news.title: Iran threatens to target US bases in Europe
news.text:
An Iranian official has threatened strikes on US bases in Europe if Donald Trump launches new strikes against Iran.

Speaking to Al Mayadeen, a Beirut-based news channel with links to Hezbollah, Iranian Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said that any base from which American aircraft take off is at risk of being attacked. 

“If the Americans make a mistake and attack us, we will not limit ourselves to nearby bases,” said Mr Rezaei. “We may even target some American military bases in European countries.”

Before the statement, US president Donald Trump had said future strikes on Iran are “unlikely”, but then added that the US is “locked and loaded” if the situation changes.

Although Iranian officials have expressed doubt over the US president’s statement, Mr Trump may be serious about ending the war with Iran given the anti-war sentiment expressed by mid-term election voters. 

Many newly elected Democrats have said they will vote to end the war, and vice president JD Vance said he believes the war was the central cause of the Republicans’ seismic defeat in the mid-terms. 

Three men who are accused of being Iran-backed operatives are facing charges in the US for attempting a terror attack on RAF Fairford, an airforce base in England which held American planes and hosted American service members. 

The US has now removed its bombers from the base. Iran has denied any involvement in the alleged plot. 

The US has 31 bases in Europe, and also shares 18 bases with European allies. 

There were approximately 84,000 US service members across the United States European Command (EUCOM) area of responsibility as of early 2025, according to data from the Centre for European Policy Analysis.

The US Air Force operates in Britain out of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall. However, the US armed forces removed several aircraft from RAF Mildenhall on November 10 amid unspecified threats.

The threat to bomb military bases in Europe is not the only major threat made by Iran against the Trump administration in recent weeks. 

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent had to move out of his Washington DC home and on to a military base in early November due to threats from Iran, according to the New York Times.

Mr Bessent has been leading financial pressure such as increased sanctions against the nation. It is unclear how severe the threats are at this time.
news.author: Sophie Clark

news.title: Progress on Ukraine-Russia peace talks despite differences over territory
news.text:
Negotiators for Russia and Ukraine emerged from a second day of US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday confident about progress towards a long-awaited peace deal, despite lingering differences over territory.

Russia’s chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said mutual understanding had been achieved on some issues and that more talks would be held, adding that the two sides had agreed on a large-scale prisoner swap.

Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said that there was “good momentum” towards reaching a solution by the end of this year, but that Europe should also be represented in future discussions.

This week’s talks in the United Arab Emirates marked a restart for diplomacy some nine months after delegations last met in Geneva to discuss peace terms.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky voiced concerns in February that Kyiv was being asked “too often” to make concessions as Moscow stuck to its maximalist demands for land in Ukraine’s mineral-rich east.

The last year has seen Ukraine test Russia’s resilience with expanded strikes on major businesses and energy infrastructure across the border, piling pressure onto the Kremlin to end what has become a costly and gruelling attritional conflict.

But Moscow has benefited from concessions from an increasingly favourable US, which temporarily waived sanctions in October and cut a deal to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.

US president Donald Trump had tried to orchestrate an “energy ceasefire” between the two sides to rein in attacks on oil refineries and keep down global prices lifted by his own war with Iran.

But when Russia apparently ignored the truce last month, Ukraine restarted its attacks on Russian infrastructure and drew Mr Trump’s ire.

Kyiv subsequently reported difficulty with its Starlink communications service and officials said they were no longer receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks.

The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, and tensions since appear to have calmed: by the end of October, the US had approved the sale of 500 much needed Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine.

But in comments to NBC’s Meet the Press, Mr Zelensky acknowledged that Ukraine would not be able to “prevail” if the United States “officially” takes Russia’s side in the conflict.

Mr Trump has positioned himself as a key mediator in the conflict since returning to office last year. But he has fairly consistently argued that Ukraine will have to give up land to end the nearly five-year war.

Earlier this week, Mr Trump said he expected a peace deal, but that Ukraine was “going to end up with a little bit [of a] different shape”.

“I believe that that war is going to end and it's going to end soon. And the only reason it's going to end is because of me,” he said, assessing that the biggest obstacle to peace was “the hatred between Zelensky and [Russian president, Vladimir] Putin”.

But when negotiators met in Geneva, it was territory that emerged as the major sticking point. Russia held firm on its demand that Ukraine cede the remaining 20pc of the eastern region of Donetsk.

The front lines have moved since those talks in February. Russia then had claimed 112,884 sq km of land, according to analysis by the Institute for the Study of War. Today, that figure has shrunk marginally to 112,734 sq km.

Assessed Russian advances – land where Russian forces have operated in or launched attacks but do not control – sat at 3,794 sq km in February, and are now down to 3,750 sq km.

Ukrainian counter-offensives – “territory where Ukrainian forces are reportedly or assessed to be conducting counter-offensives or counter-attacks” – have swollen from 59,800 sq km in February to 70,222 sq km in November, according to the same source.

Changes on the battlefield are reflected in changes in technology and tactics behind the scenes. Russia went into the war with the range advantage, hosting stockpiles of ballistic missiles and access to long-range Shahed drones as early as summer 2022.

Those Iranian-made drones can travel up to 2,000km with a 50kg warhead.

That advantage gave Moscow the ability to thrash morale in Ukraine’s major cities, destroy warehouses full of munitions, and devastate energy infrastructure deep behind enemy lines.

But Ukraine today says its weapons are destroying targets some 1,750km away – up from 630km in 2022.

Kyiv says its strategy of targeting Russian energy facilities is aimed at sapping a key source of Russia’s war funds and showing Russians the conflict started by Moscow is closer to home than ever. In these objectives, it has been effective.

As of November 10, analysts estimate that around 30pc of Russia’s total oil-processing capacity has been knocked offline or disrupted. That figure is a jump from 20pc reported only in June.

“This level of disruption is unprecedented in the history of the Russia-Ukraine conflict,” the IEA said over the summer.
news.summary: Sides agree on a large-scale prisoner swap
news.author: James C Reynolds

news.title: The Irish Independent’s View: Gathering of leaders is chance to show a way that remains true to principles of democracy
news.text:
Russian tanks rolling over the Ukrainian border in February 2022 gave real impetus to build a larger community of democratic nations to cooperate in defence of liberty. This illegal and immoral war reinforced efforts to create what became the European Political Community (EPC).

Today’s historic meeting of 47 world leaders in Dublin, under the aegis of Ireland’s EU presidency, shows that the EPC has the potential to do good in an increasingly dangerous world. The body is committed to practical support for democracy and prosperity.

But this welcome continuation of meetings by the world’s democratic leaders is not an end in itself. People in far too many countries have lost faith in mainstream democratic politics and are turning to dangerous extremes on the hard-left, and especially the hard-right.

Many of the leaders attending today applauded the huge mid-term election reverses for Donald Trump. But the US president will continue nominally in office for two more years, adding to a sense of global drift and a lack of leadership.

The leaders gathered in Dublin must send a strong message of hope to people who risk totally losing faith in democracy and who fear the rule of law and human rights are up for grabs. These leaders must show the real potential for a different pole of world political power through unity and a spirit of common purpose.

Liberty, democracy and prosperity must remain the cornerstone values.

news.title: Russell Brand's Instagram disabled but cryptic ‘stay tuned’ message appears on X
news.text: Russell Brand's Instagram account has been deactivated, but posts continue to emerge on his X account as he serves a prison sentence for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Wednesday, November 11, the comedian's verified account, @rustyrockets, had a dig at Meta and posted images displaying his Instagram account being shut down. "There never was a Russell Brand , according to @Meta. Thank God for @elonmusk. Stay tuned," the post read. It remained unclear who penned the message or was operating the account while Brand, 51, was behind bars. Meta told TMZ that Brand's Instagram account had been taken down because it "violates our policies.", reports the Mirror US . That policy permits Meta to restrict or disable accounts belonging to individuals who "engage in off-platform activity that can lead to harm." Convicted sex offenders are amongst those covered by the rule. The X post displayed Brand's Facebook page next to a notice stating the Facebook page had been suspended. The X account stayed active following the Meta suspensions, delivering the message to Brand's followers. The account ban arrived after Brand was sentenced Monday, November 9, in London to 10 years and six months in prison. A jury convicted him on November 5 of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week trial. Brand pleaded not guilty and denied wrongdoing. Donald Trump Jr. leapt to Brand's defence on Tuesday's episode of his Triggered show, claiming the comedian had been targeted because of his newfound religious beliefs and shift towards conservative politics. He said: "When he was like married to Katy Perry, he's one of the most famous actors in the world, no one seemed to have a problem. No one seemed to think he was a rapist then. But he finds God, I guess, changes his ways, sees some aspects of conservative life and talks about them. "And now he's going to spend ... years in prison for rape when no one had a problem with it in the prior 27 years." Police paid tribute to the women who came forward to report Brand following the verdict. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy described the outcome as "first and foremost a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them. "Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us," he said. "Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible."
news.summary: Russell Brand's Instagram account has been disabled by Meta, but posts are still appearing on his X account as he serves a 10-year-and-six-month jail sentence for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault
news.author: Connor McCrory,Paige Ingram

news.title: Scott Colom Wins Mississippi, Becomes State's 1st Black Senator Since 1874
news.text: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any US state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.The Associated Press called the contest Wednesday in Colom's favor after local elections officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi."While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," Hyde-Smith, 67, said in a two-minute concession speech posted online. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state."A spokesman for the senator said she called Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly.READ | Saba Haider Credits Ghaziabad Upbringing For Her Public Life, US WinColom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson.The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith's missteps as she sought a second full term."They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society."It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America - a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.Party leaders hailed the senator-elect's triumph, with nods to the South's emerging battleground status after other upset victories from North Carolina to Texas."Scott Colom is the only person who could've gotten this done," Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online. "Along with his staff and volunteers, Scott ran the campaign of a lifetime and re-imagined what's possible for Democrats in the South."Former President Bill Clinton, a native Arkansan who campaigned with Colom days before the election, addressed the senator-elect on social media, saying he won "because you believe in the promise of your state's people. And they believed in you right back."Vera Finley was among those supporters, and she arrived early Wednesday to Colom's victory party."I am here to celebrate my parents and my grandparents. I am not one generation out of the cotton fields," Finley said. "Both of my parents picked cotton. And my great grandmother was sold here as a slave from Virginia to here. So I am so excited to be on this side of history."Another Mississippian, NAACP President Derrick Johnson, issued a statement saying the state's voters "made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out.""In a state that has witnessed some of the nation's most difficult battles for voting rights, Black voters once again demonstrated the power of civic engagement and the strength of our democracy," Johnson said.Despite Schumer's support, the contest was a latecomer to the national spotlight, finally drawing attention and money months after Black senators, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock and Maryland's Angela Alsobrooks, first urged donors and party leaders to see Mississippi as winnable.The son of a onetime Republican who worked for President Ronald Reagan, Colom garnered attention for his aggressive campaign as Democrats widened the Senate battleground map and Hyde-Smith's vulnerabilities crystallized.He produced of the year's most widely circulated ads. After Hyde-Smith seemed to brush off high beef prices by saying consumers could choose other proteins, Colom cut a 30-second spot depicting incredulous voters saying they'd "pick another senator instead."When Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, in late October for a rally with Hyde-Smith, Colom walked the line of Trump supporters as they waited outside the gates. He introduced himself, asked about their concerns and explained his priorities.Later that evening, when Trump called Hyde-Smith to the stage, she said nine words in six seconds: "Is this not the best president in our lifetime?"Then she stepped away.Colom's appearance outside the rally tracked his strategy of criticizing Trump's policies - especially the Iran war and tariffs that he said were especially hard on Mississippi farmers - without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Instead, he consistently put the onus on Hyde-Smith, framing her as a nonentity in Washington - a critique that resonated in a state accustomed to long-serving senators like Thad Cochran, Trent Lott and John Stennis, who all rose to powerful posts and routed federal money back to Mississippi.There is some irony to Hyde-Smith losing to Colom. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom to be a US District Court judge in the Northern District of Mississippi. Mississippi's senior Republican Sen. Roger Wicker and former Governor Haley Barbour, who is also a former national Republican chairman, backed the nomination.Hyde-Smith, however, blocked Colom's confirmation under the Senate tradition that members can spike a president's choices for federal judicial positions in their home state. Colom said his campaign was never about getting even with Hyde-Smith.The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist and died in front of his family."In Mississippi, no one is above the law, and no one should be outside its protection," Colom said, telling the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction."He was killed for helping Mississippians vote," Colom said. "On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right."Schumer helped Colom raise money, and he drew financial support from other outside players, including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire and potential presidential candidate.Former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned on Colom's behalf in the campaign's closing weeks.Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours. Trump won by double digits in each of his three presidential contests, but in 2023, Republican Governor Tate Reeves managed to win reelection by a margin of just 3 percentage points.Colom and other Black party leaders and strategists insisted throughout 2026 that he could narrow the gap with strong Black turnout, Republican voter discontent and an uptick in Democrats' usual share of the white vote in Mississippi.Results showed strong turnout in the Mississippi Delta and its concentration of majority Black counties. But nearly all of the state moved leftward from the 2024 election, when Trump carried Mississippi by nearly 23 points.Then-Governor Phil Bryant first appointed Hyde-Smith, who was state agriculture commissioner, to the Senate in 2018 when Cochran resigned. She won a special election runoff in 2018 and a full term in 2020. Both times she defeated Democrat Mike Espy, a former US agriculture secretary who'd also been Mississippi's first Black congressman since Reconstruction.During the extended vote count, Colom acknowledged the historic nature of doing what Espy could not. But he said he sees his place more in terms of other Mississippians, especially its youngest residents, than his individual story."My job is to do well enough as the next United States senator that the next time some young Black boy or girl has the work ethic, the vision, and the values," he said, "and they want to be United States senator, that nobody says because of anything I've done that they shouldn't get a chance."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Because of the Black population and its alignment with Democrats, Mississippi's general elections have been closer for years than its immediate Southern neighbours.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Red State GOP Organizations Need to Get Their Act Together
news.text:
There’s no one fatter and lazier than a deep red state’s Republican organization, with few exceptions, and this bit us badly on the butt last week. Now, California is not a red state — not anymore, though it was when I grew up there — but this little story kind of sums up the problem with Republican organizations. They aren’t about winning; they are social clubs. I was at some GOP event and sat down for rubber chicken next to somebody who proudly announced he was the Republican chair of, say, the 69th District and had been for 20 years. I asked him when the last time a Republican won in the 69th District was, and he looked at me like I was insane, like it never occurred to him that electing people might be a remotely relevant consideration for a district chair. The answer, of course, was “Never.” The Republicans had never won it. But he had his gig, a nice seat on the dais, and that was what mattered. Not victory. Just his place in the social club that is the California Republican Party.

In the red states, we got too used to winning easily. Far too used to it. We got so used to winning that it never occurred to us that we might not win, and it never occurred to us that we might have to work to win. We forgot that we need to earn votes, that we don’t just inherit them by right. Sure, some marquee candidates were awful, but it wasn’t just the marquee candidates who lost. It was everyone from governors down to assistant deputy dog catchers. If you had an R by your name, you were about as popular as an openly herpetic participant in a polycule orgy.

Here’s the thing. We got soft. When you are challenged, when you don’t have to fight – and even when you do (Hi, California) – you run the risk of your organization becoming sclerotic, petrified, and wussified. The last part, the wussy part, is particularly important. In a deep red state, where it was difficult (before this year) to get elected anything if you weren’t a Republican, a lot of people who should be Democrats were joining the GOP. That’s how we get squishes. That’s why we get RINOs. John Cornyn has always been a Republican, but it should be no surprise that he helped Democrats with things like gun control, and that he eagerly helped, in the feminine and sneaky way of his ilk, to get James Talarico elected by undercutting the actual Republican nominee and then rushing to congratulate the Democrat. Now, all ex-Democrats aren’t bad – both Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump started out as Democrats – but joining the GOP because they’ve had a change of heart is different from joining because you think it’s to your advantage. That’s how you end up with extremely soft Republicans.

Another is having no fear of the voters. Too many red incumbents think they can’t be dislodged from their sinecures. Look at James Lankford in Oklahoma. It’s no surprise that a clueless tool like Jimmy colluded with the Democrats on a border bill that critics said would effectively allow 5,000 encounters a day before emergency authority kicked in. He gave the other side huge assistance, and it never occurred to him that it might put his seat at risk. He’s up for reelection in 2028. Of course, he’s going to get primaried — he’s like the buffalo with a limp as the wolves circle. But is he going to do the manly thing and refuse to run rather than put the GOP through an expensive primary so it can get a Republican who actually does Republican things in office? Absolutely not. The idea of selfless service is completely alien to this archetype. We voters are there to serve them, not vice versa. You see the problem?

You look at a state like Utah, and you would think that a state full of Mormons should be a state full of hard-driving conservatives. They’ve got one, Mike Lee, but holy cow, John Curtis is an absolute disaster. He’s a posturing twit who makes Mitt Romney look like Genghis Khan. And their governor, Spencer Cox, plays footsie with the trans weirdos. How did this happen?

Again, if everybody’s a Republican, then everybody’s a Republican. And that means people who shouldn’t be Republicans, too. I guess if you’re looking to make lemonade out of this lemon suppository, one good thing is that you might see Democrats joining the Democrat Party in red states that had a blue spasm. But who still holds all the key positions? The people who’ve been there forever. The people who’ve never been challenged, and when they were challenged this year, they failed with flying colors.

Look at Indiana. There’s a state that should be ruby red, but enough of its state legislators refused to do their part to gerrymander the districts to a Republican advantage. Why? Because principles or something. It never occurred to them to be team players because they considered themselves the team. It wasn’t about them serving the people through the Republican Party. It was about the people serving them through the Republican Party.

It just never occurred to them that they had to fight. They thought they'd get wins handed to them on a silver platter. The Texas Republicans sure did. What did Greg Abbott do in his campaign? I think I saw one ad for him. Was he out there connecting with the voters whom he had governed for 12 years? Apparently not. What’s frightening is that maybe he thought he was going to win, and maybe the other Republicans thought they were going to win, too. How could we get so out of touch with our own voters? Hey, I’m not taking myself off the blame list – as a pundit, I thought we were going to do a lot better than we did. But the rumblings were out there. The clues were out there. The guys and gals who work with the grassroots every day should’ve seen that many of the people they expected to show up either weren't going to show up or were angry/desperate enough to give the Democrats a chance.

And then there’s the treachery. In Texas, you had this whole group of establishment swells within the Republican orbit, ex-Bush types, who had absolutely no loyalty to the people who had been loyal to them. They had nothing but contempt for voters. The voters were supposed to shut up and pull the lever. Well, the voters shut up to the pollsters and pulled the lever for the other guys. And the Bush types, at some level, are happy about it. They think this is their way back in. If we don’t fight these clowns off, it will be.

Mississippi was a heartbreaker and a headscratcher. Did you know the Democrat Senate candidate spent far more on ads and organization than our clueless Republican incumbent? And they organized the hell out of their people. We didn’t. We didn’t even bother. We just assumed we'd win. Even in the post-election ballot counting, the Democrats have everything lined up, from lawyers to vote-count watchers. The Republicans have barely scraped together a team to respond. This is the Republican Party of Mississippi. These are the people in charge. And they didn’t do anything. It’s a disaster.

This must stop. The Republican Party is not a social club. It has one purpose and one purpose only, and it’s not to provide a venue for activists to high-five each other. It’s to win elections. That’s it. That’s all. It’s not for making friends or padding résumés. It’s to beat the Democrats and save this country.

Republicans in Florida understand that. The Republicans in Florida worked. Look at those registration numbers they’ve put up there. It’s a majority Republican state. You couldn’t say that 26 years ago. Remember hanging chads? I do. It was purple back then. Democrats used to win in Florida. news.title: Trump Is Right: Ukraine Needs a Leader Who Can Close the Deal
news.text:
After nearly five years of war, the question is no longer only who can defend Ukraine. It is who can negotiate a peace that lasts.

In late October, something rare happened in Ukraine: Russian and Ukrainian forces held their fire around the town of Oleshky so civilians could get out.

The localized ceasefire, brokered by First Lady Melania Trump, let aid reach residents who had gone months without power, water or reliable food. Evacuees reached safety, and Newsmax cameras documented the operation. 

Oleshky did not end the war. But it proved that even bitter enemies can reach agreements when there is political will, effective mediation and a clearly defined objective.

Now comes the harder question: who can turn limited breakthroughs into a lasting peace?

Trump’s Challenge

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal...” President Donald Trump said on October 10. On Newsmax’s “Finnerty,” he called Zelensky “not a good guy for us to deal with.”

Zelensky deserves credit for rallying Ukrainians and securing Western support, and his government cooperated in Oleshky. But defending a country and ending a war demand different skills. The question is whether he will, or can, deliver a comprehensive settlement, one requiring painful decisions on territory and security, public trust and political legitimacy.

Does Zelensky Want This War to End?

Trump’s frustration reflects a pattern. On October 11, he announced an energy ceasefire. Within days, Zelensky declared Kyiv “done” with it, resumed strikes on Russian refineries and said he would stop again only if Washington supplied Patriot interceptors. Kyiv says Russia kept hitting its power grid, a fair complaint. But Zelensky ended a truce the American president had announced and named his price for another. Trump called the strikes “a disgrace” and told Newsmax he finds Zelensky “more difficult to deal with than Putin.”

Zelensky’s offers, such as freezing the current front line, are ones Moscow has already rejected. He says Ukrainians would reject any deal handing Russia the rest of Donbas. Each position lets Kyiv look flexible while the war grinds on.

His defenders blame Moscow, and Russia’s demands are indeed extreme. But a leader determined to end a war prepares his public for compromise. Zelensky has done the reverse. His record is that of a leader who finds reasons to keep fighting, not ways to stop.

Ukrainians Are Questioning Their Leadership

The leadership debate is not confined to Washington.

Vadym Novynskyi, a prominent Ukrainian businessman, former parliamentarian and Orthodox protodeacon living in European exile, called in October for Zelensky’s resignation and a parliamentary role in launching direct peace talks.

Novynskyi says he helped organize the April 2022 Istanbul negotiations and believes they presented an opportunity for compromise. “But Zelensky chose the path of war,” he wrote. He argues that Zelensky abandoned the peace platform behind his roughly 73 percent victory in the 2019 runoff.

“Zelensky will never agree to the end of the war, and his stay in power is a guarantee that the war will continue,” Novynskyi said, warning that prolonged fighting could imperil Ukrainian statehood.

Novynskyi has his own dispute with Kyiv: Zelensky sanctioned him in December 2022; his businesses faced searches, frozen assets and suspended gas licenses. Ukrainian authorities allege wrongdoing and later accused him of treason and other offenses. Novynskyi describes political retaliation and a crackdown on his church.

Lawmaker Oleksiy Goncharenko argues that Ukraine is losing a war of attrition. Rather than settle everything at once, he proposes a series of smaller agreements on shipping, energy and civilian infrastructure. Oleshky is a working example of that approach.

The Mandate Problem

Zelensky’s five-year term expired in May 2024. Elections are suspended under martial law, and he has called a wartime vote a “tsunami” that would split the country. There is a case for caution. But it leaves Ukraine negotiating its future through a president whose term has lapsed and whose office is under a cloud.

In November 2025, chief of staff and lead negotiator Andriy Yermak resigned hours after anti-corruption investigators searched his home; in May, they named him a suspect in a money-laundering case. In August, Zelensky fired deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra as investigators targeted an alleged money-laundering ring involving his office. 

Zelensky himself has not been accused of wrongdoing, and Ukraine’s independent anti-corruption agencies deserve credit for pursuing these cases. But in 2025 his own government moved to curb those agencies’ independence, backing down only after public protests.

America First Means Delivering Results

Trump’s challenge is not an American demand to pick Ukraine’s next president. That decision belongs to Ukrainians.

But Washington is entitled to ask what its support is achieving. After over $175 billion in aid related to Ukraine, approved under President Joe Biden, “stay the course” is no answer.

On October 11, Zelensky told ABC’s “This Week” that Ukraine would hold elections if Putin agreed to a full 60-day ceasefire. The Kremlin rejected the idea. Washington should not let it die. If a ceasefire can be brokered for one town, the United States can put an election ceasefire on the table at the Abu Dhabi talks expected this month. Moscow questions Zelensky’s legitimacy; Zelensky says he is ready to face voters. Both claims can be tested.

Peace should also deliver for Americans. It should deter another Russian attack and keep America out of a direct clash with Moscow. It should hold Europe to its pledge of 5 percent of GDP for defense by 2035, delivered as ammunition, air defenses and deployable forces. It should free American arms and intelligence for the Indo-Pacific, where China is the bigger long-term challenge. And it should open doors for American business, from possible projects in Arctic energy and critical minerals to the minerals and reconstruction deal Washington already has with Kyiv.

An endless war is not a strategy. A rushed agreement that invites another invasion is not peace.

After years of sacrifice, Ukraine needs more than a president who can sustain international support for its war effort. It needs a leader with the mandate to turn that support into a peace that lasts.

news.title: Stephen Miller: Superstar
news.text:
When Stephen Miller first appeared on my radio show as a high school teenager, did I see his potential? I've been asked this many times.

Stephen, then a student at California's Santa Monica High School, contacted my radio show with a complaint. California's Education Code requires elementary, middle and high schools to conduct "a patriotic ritual," like citing the Pledge of Allegiance, at the beginning of each school day. Santa Monica High was not doing this. Stephen complained, without success, to his teachers, the principal and administrators.

So, he called my show, cited the Education Code and talked about the value of the pledge as a way of teaching students to understand the principles upon which our "American exceptionalism" was founded. That his school was "blatantly" disregarding this "patriotic obligation," Stephen argued, does not bode well for the nation. He created a groundswell. People who had graduated from that high school years ago, when the pledge was cited, called the school to complain.

Over the next several years, Stephen appeared on my show 69 times. (He counted them.) He was passionate, funny, intense, articulate and extremely knowledgeable. He dressed like a Wall Street lawyer. He complained bitterly about his school's use of "A People's History of the United States" by left-wing historian Howard Zinn. "The book," Stephen said, "has given a generation a warped sense of history by focusing on America's dark chapters, as opposed to viewing this nation as a work in progress to become a more perfect union."

Stephen attended Duke University, when members of the men's lacrosse team were accused of raping a stripper. While many at Duke pronounced the "privileged" young men guilty, Stephen told my audience the charges were bogus and that the "crusading" prosecutor, who publicly pronounced them guilty, was ignoring exculpatory evidence. The charges were dropped. The prosecutor lost his job and law license and served a day in prison for withholding evidence.

After Duke, Stephen became a staffer for Alabama Sen. Jeff Sessions. At the time, I visited Stephen in D.C., where we walked around and Stephen said, "If you could wave a magic wand and eliminate this building, that building and that building, no one would notice. There's so much stuff going on in this town that is completely pointless."

Sessions, with Stephen's advice, became a loud critic of "chain migration," the potential of limitless immigration through a succession of family memberships. In 2015, Sessions "loaned" Stephen to then-presidential candidate Donald Trump. Sessions never got him back.

Stephen has advised Trump on domestic policy, including immigration. Stephen's influence is such that he has long likely been Trump's chief of staff in all but name. Now it's official.

After his first few appearances on my show, Stephen and I became friends. I met Chris, Stephen's close friend and classmate, who convinced Stephen, then a self-described liberal — like virtually everyone in Santa Monica — to re-think his assumptions. Chris, now a lawyer, laughingly told me, "I created a monster."

Stephen's parents told me they, too, were once liberals before Stephen convinced them they were not. Stephen's father called me his son's "mentor." I said, "If you mean politics, that title goes to Chris. But thank you."

Stephen invited me to speak at his high school, but "negotiations" dragged on for months. The school administration insisted that another speaker must later be invited "to provide balance."

On the day of my speech, Stephen and I met with the principal. I told her the school permitted a left-wing union leader to speak earlier this semester. "Did you follow up her speech," I asked, "with a conservative speaker 'to provide balance'?"

The principal squirmed before reluctantly admitting that, well, no, she did not. Stephen was delighted. "That was beautiful. You nailed her!" he said after we left her office. "This bias has got to stop! It's hurting the country."

Stephen saw a career in politics, but not as a politician. He wanted to influence policy, to make sure Americans understand that our republic is not guaranteed.

Did I see that he would become the chief of staff to a president of the United States? No, not quite.

But when this effervescent high school student asked me where I thought he would go in life, I said, "Stephen, to borrow a quote from Oprah Winfrey, your future is so bright it blinds my eyes."

news.title: TIMELINE: Trump's ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in the spotlight
news.text:
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump's close ties with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ​have come under renewed scrutiny after revelations about the billionaire executive's affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Trump said on Monday he was "amazed" after the revelations concerning one of his closest allies in Silicon Valley, who also faces an FBI probe as well as a board meeting to decide his future.

Over the past two years, Huang has voiced support for the Trump administration's AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market and lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to Nvidia's sophisticated AI chips.

Democratic and Republican lawmakers have called to halt exports of advanced AI chips to China. Huang and the White House have argued that continuing US sales to China would keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology.

Here is a timeline on some publicly known interactions and meetings between the Nvidia CEO and Trump since the Republican leader returned to the White House in January 2025:

JANUARY 2025:

Trump met the Nvidia boss during the first month of his return to the White House, casting the interaction as a good meeting.

The Nvidia CEO met Trump at the White House before Huang's visit to China.

Later in the month, Trump gave a shout out to Huang as he spoke and signed executive orders at an AI summit.

"Jensen, will you stand up? What a job, what a job you've done," Trump remarked. "He's a great guy too."

AUGUST 2025:

Huang met Trump at the White House as the Trump administration and Nvidia engaged in talks over allowing advanced AI chip sales to China.

SEPTEMBER 2025:

Huang joined Trump during a state visit to Britain.

NOVEMBER 2025:

The Nvidia CEO attended a US-Saudi Arabia investment forum in Washington during the first visit of Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the US capital since 2018. Huang talked about the future of AI at the event.

DECEMBER 2025:

Trump praised Huang when the Nvidia CEO visited Washington and met the Republican leader, who said the chip executive was aware of where he stood on export controls.

Huang was in the US capital that day to meet lawmakers and told them that state-by-state US regulations would slow the progress of AI development.

JANUARY 2026:

The Trump administration began allowing some exports of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China on a case-by-case basis but it did not lift the restrictions applying to organizations that Washington had put on a trade restriction list.

MARCH 2026:

In late March, the White House announced Huang as part of a 13-member council formally called the "President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology" to weigh in on AI policy and other issues.

Huang was among a delegation of tech CEOs who joined Trump during his visit to China to meet Xi as the Republican leader aimed to urge Beijing to "open up" to US business.

Trump, in a last minute addition to his May trip to China, asked Huang to join him. The Nvidia CEO was spotted boarding Air Force One during a re-fuelling stop in Alaska en route to Beijing.

SEPTEMBER 2026:

As the Trump administration and AI companies faced increasing scrutiny over risks posed by advanced AI, Trump said on September 29 that Huang was among a number of AI CEOs who signed a voluntary safety pact and backed data center expansion.

Huang met Trump at the White House that day along with a number of tech executives. Trump, who had argued previously that the US ​does ⁠not need new AI-specific regulations, said the pact was "morally binding," prompting criticism that it did not lay out consequences for non-compliance.

In the previous week, Huang attended a high-profile state dinner for Xi Jinping at the White House when the Chinese president met Trump.

In mid-September, the Nvidia CEO addressed AI safety concerns during a summit in Los Angeles. He took a phone call from Trump during the event and put him on speaker for the audience. During the roughly five-minute call, Trump called AI safety fears a "hoax."

OCTOBER 2026:

In early October, Trump awarded the National Medal of Science, the United States' highest honor for scientists and engineers, to the Nvidia CEO and some other tech industry leaders.

The same day Trump gave the Nvidia CEO the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million in Nvidia stock during the summer of 2026.

The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $25 million for Trump's planned White House ballroom.

NOVEMBER 2026:

Trump said he spoke to the Nvidia boss after the affair between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang - an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, whom US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset - became public.

Trump said on November 9 the Nvidia CEO told him he had no idea that the woman was a spy and that Trump believed the CEO.

"I asked him that question 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea that she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told a White House briefing.

"I know the FBI is looking into it," Trump said. "I think that he'll be in good shape."

news.title: EU leaders shamed for missing climate summit to attend Dublin gathering
news.text: United Nations chief António Guterres yesterday accused fossil fuel giants of making a financial killing while "killing our planet" — warning world leaders that humanity has reached an apocalyptic "make or bake" moment. In a blistering address on Day Three of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya where thousands of delgates and activists including Greta Thunberg have gathered, the outgoing UN Secretary-General delivered a devastating rebuke to billionaire oil barons and the no-show politicians dodging the summit. Addressing a depleted gathering of world leaders as formal talks got underway, Mr Guterres pulled no punches about the catastrophic reality facing our boiling world. "Our first climate duty is to tell the truth," the UN chief declared. "The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering. The last four years were the hottest ever." Railing against rampant corporate greed, he blasted: "And fossil fuel interests keep making a killing … while killing our planet. “ Climate disasters are pounding lives, livelihoods and economies across the globe. This is the path to mutually assured destruction." Mr Guterres warned the assembly that global temperature rise will now inevitably overshoot the critical 1.5C threshold agreed 11 years ago in Paris. But he insisted humanity cannot throw in the towel. "Science tells us an overshoot above that level is now inevitable," he insisted. "But science is not telling us to surrender. It’s telling us to fight harder. “The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be. We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence." Taking aim at the armies of corporate lobbyists swarming climate policy, Mr Guterres unleashed a blistering comparison: " Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs," he warned. "But that won’t happen on its own. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. But fossil fuels do. And their strategy is simple: Distort the science. Delay the policy. Delay the action. Delay the accountability. It’s time to kick the habit – and end the fossil-fuel addiction." With current national pledges putting the planet on track for a catastrophic 2.5C rise by century's end, Mr Guterres warned: "Our planet is heating up . The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time." Mr Guterres urged world governments to slap windfall taxes on mega-rich oil companies to bankroll frontline nations drowning in climate chaos. Exposing the staggering financial divide, he revealed: "In the last quarter alone, the nine largest oil companies pocketed $95 billion in profits. “Meanwhile, the Loss and Damage Fund has received around $600 million. That is what these companies made in about 14 hours. "It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits – and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay." Backing up the Secretary-General, UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell warned political leaders at an afternoon plenary that rampant fossil fuel reliance i s driving ordinary working families to the wall. "Today, chaos in global energy markets and climate disasters are supercharging inflation: Slamming government budgets, pushing household bills up and living standards down," Mr Stiell said. "The political costs of fossil fuel dependency are unforgiving." He told ministers: "Clean energy means secure energy and more sustainable and stable economies – protected from fossil fuel volatility. Please, tell your ministers we cannot leave Antalya without a strong negotiated outcome." In a heartbreaking speech that silenced the main plenary hall, Surangel Whipps Jr., President of the tiny Pacific island nation of Palau, lashed out at rich polluting nations. "You might as well bomb us. That might have been easier than watching climate change tear apart our homes piece by piece," President Whipps said. "We are at war with a crisis we did not create. A war no peace treaty can end, only urgent action can." Micronesian President Wesley Simina warned that his homeland is suffering irreversible losses of coral reefs that "protect our shores, sustain our fisheries, feed our families and carry the stories and traditions of our communities." Warning that global warming is the "single greatest threat to the security, livelihoods, and well-being of Pacific peoples," President Simina pleaded: "Every fraction of a degree counts. Every fraction avoided reduces risk... This is why the world must act not only deeply, but quickly." The human toll was underlined by Amy Pope, Director General of the International Organization for Migration, who revealed that climate-fuelled disasters displaced nearly 30 million people in 2025 alone. Yet as frontline leaders wept for their homelands, the halls of the Turkish venue echoed with the deafening absence of the planet's biggest polluters. The leaders of China, the United States, and India — who together spew out more than half of the world's carbon emissions — boycotted yesterday's Leaders' Summit entirely. US President Donald Trump, who has branded climate change a "hoax", targeted offshore wind projects, and gutted power plant emission caps, shunned the UN talks for the second year running. European leaders also came under heavy fire for abandoning the summit. While European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attended, more than half of EU heads of state failed to show up as they were at an EU event in Dublin. Mohamed Adow, director of think tank Power Shift Africa, branded the mass no-show an absolute betrayal: "It really is a disgrace that just one of the seven G7 heads of state and only a handful of G20 leaders are attending this summit. The world's biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others." news.title: Nvidia board reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after alleged affairs
news.text:
The Nvidia board is reportedly planning to oust CEO Jensen Huang amid reports he engaged in two extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy and another with an executive at his tech company.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future with the technology giant he founded.

ABC News has reached out to Nvidia for comment.

On Sunday, Nvidia said that its board launched an independent investigation "in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

The development on Wednesday comes after The New York Times reported nearly two weeks ago that Huang had "a close relationship" with an alleged Chinese government agent, identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed. He later admitted in an internal statement to Nvidia staff that he had been "unfaithful to his wife."

Amid the fallout from the allegations and the letter, The Times reported on Wednesday that Huang also allegedly had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who allegedly reports to him.

The outlet, citing sources within the company, reported that Huang and his colleague were allegedly captured on video being affectionate at a hotel during an Nvidia conference in March. The New York Times said it had not seen the video.

ABC News has not been able to verify the reporting or the alleged video.

Following the reporting about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who are not related, the Chinese government denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."

Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.

"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an Nvidia spokesperson told ABC News at the time.

On Sunday, Nvidia shared with ABC News the internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful," apologizing for hurting his wife and family.

"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.

Addressing Nvidia staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.

Following the New York Times report, congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China sent a letter to Jensen Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang.

The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, told ABC News on Tuesday that he's prepared to subpoena Huang if he does not respond by Wednesday to a request from several House Republicans.

President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that he spoke with Huang that day about the allegations.

"I asked him that question -- 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy,' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

In its statement on Sunday, Nvidia said that a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement further said.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," according to the statement.

"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement further said.

"The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team," according to the statement.

Nvidia has grown to be one of the most important chip makers in recent years due to its components being key to AI computing servers.
news.summary: The Nvidia board is reportedly planning to oust CEO Jensen Huang amid reports he engaged in two extramarital affairs.

news.title: Jim Jordan Says Democrats Will Target Entire Trump Cabinet, 2028 Nominee
news.text: Republican Jim Jordan, the newly elected House minority leader, said on Wednesday night that the Democratic Party will "go after" President Donald Trump's entire Cabinet and probably target the GOP 2028 nominee, after sweeping midterm election wins that flipped both House and Senate majority in Democrats' favor. "There’ll be a third impeachment. They can’t help themselves. They’re going to go after everyone in the Cabinet. We’ve already seen that with Secretary of War [Pete] Hegseth," Jordan told Fox News' Sean Hannity. "I think what they’re probably going to also do, I think they're gonna go after whoever they think our nominee is going to be. Will they go after Vice President [JD] Vance? Will they go after Secretary [Marco] Rubio, Governor [Ron] DeSantis, Governor [Glenn] Youngkin...whoever they think might be our nominee? I think you’ll see them target them." Jordan's remarks come after a failed vote to refer Republican Representative Thomas Massie’s eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth forward on Tuesday. President Donald Trump, the White House and other Republicans celebrated the unsuccessful attempt at facilitating the removal of Hegseth from his position, as Democrats all but assured another effort to impeach the defense secretary will occur next year. When asked if Democrats should push to impeach Hegseth in the new Congress, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told CNN in part, "There are so many criminals in this administration, it’s hard to figure out...the order of operations. There are going to be many, many, many investigations. news.title: Ukraine and Russia agree to large-scale prisoner exchange after second day of talks
news.text:
Ukraine and Russia agreed to a prisoner swap during talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, according to reports. 

The US-brokered negotiations are the first to take place since February, when Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu launched an offensive against Iran, derailing progress on a potential ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow. 

A large-scale prisoner swap has also been agreed during the discussions and may take place between the next two to three weeks, according to Russian news agency TASS citing Russian Lieutenant-General Alexander Zorin. 

Zorin said that the exchange would consist of more than 1,000 prisoners on each side. 

After the first day of talks US secretary of state Marco Rubio said that “a lot” of work was still to be done. 

Russia’s chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said that mutual understanding had been achieved on some issues but that more talks are yet to be held to iron out differences. 

It follows claims by Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky that the US agreed with Ukraine’s assessment of what was happening on the battlefield and that Vladimir Putin lived in a “different reality”.

The Ukrainian leader said Russia had claimed that it held half of the Donbas region in Ukraine’s east.

“Putin lives in a different reality,” Zelensky said. “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true.”

However, he added that the second day of talks was “constructive and quite substantive”. 

The discussions are the first of their kind in nine months as the US has been occupied with the conflict in Iran. Delegations from Moscow and Kyiv met for the two-day talks on Tuesday and Wednesday. 

Washington was represented by special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law and businessman Jared Kushner. The talks are reported to have lasted four hours. 

Last week, Mariana Katzarova, UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Russia, said that at least 438 Ukrainians have died in Russian captivity and that torture and ill-treatment of prisoners is systematic. 

The United Nations estimates that around 16,000 Ukrainian citizens are being held in Russian captivity. 

Speaking at the Munich Security Conference in February earlier this year, Zelensky said that around 7,000 Ukrainians were being held in Russian captivity and 4,000 Russians in Ukrainian detention. 

More than 95 per cent of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85 per cent of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, according to UN officials. 

Past talks between Russia and Ukraine have yielded little progress with key sticking points including territory and security guarantees.
news.summary: Thousands of Ukrainians are held in Russian captivity

news.title: Iran Warns It May Target U.S. Military Bases Across Europe
news.text:
Iran has issued a sweeping warning to the United States: if American forces use bases outside the Middle East to launch strikes on Iranian territory, Tehran says those facilities could become targets as well — including installations in Europe.

Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s security chief, delivered the threat in an interview broadcast today by Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen TV. “If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well,” Mr Rezaei said.

He said any renewed US assault would prompt Iran to expand its response to what he called “America’s more distant military installations – including the ones we have not yet attacked,” though he did not identify specific locations.

“We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles,” he added. The interview was conducted in Tehran.

The Middle East war began on 28 February, when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Iran retaliated by firing missiles and drones at countries across the region, and militant groups backed by Tehran in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq also joined the fight.

Even as the conflict has widened, Qatar and Pakistan have been leading diplomatic efforts aimed at negotiating an end to the war.

Tehran has insisted Washington agree to a package of demands — including unfreezing Iranian assets and lifting sanctions — in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial energy corridor that Iran has blockaded since the conflict began.

The US and Israel have repeatedly pointed to Iran’s nuclear programme as part of their rationale for the war. But Mr Rezaei said the nuclear issue was “not currently” part of the talks, and he outlined what he described as firm Iranian red lines, including that Iran would “not send even a tiny amount of the enriched material outside Iran”.

Iran’s nuclear programme — and its stockpile of uranium enriched up to 60%, near the 90% level needed for an atomic bomb — has fuelled tensions for years.

Yesterday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no need to attack Iran again, pointing instead to what he described as successful efforts to weaken Iran’s economy.

Washington has appeared to scale back recent warnings of fresh strikes after President Donald Trump’s Republican party lost in recent midterm elections, a setback attributed in part to the war’s unpopularity.

Trump defends Iran war in Veterans Day address

US President Donald Trump salutes during a ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery

President Donald Trump used a Veterans Day event today to argue that the war is justified and nearing an end.

“The bravery and skill of our amazing American warriors has absolutely been incredible,” Mr Trump said in remarks at Arlington National Cemetery just outside Washington.

“When this conflict is over, and it will be soon, the entire world will be a much safer and better place, more peaceful place, and a place without the kind of danger that we had to suffer.”

The war has killed 23 US service members and wounded several hundred more, according to the latest Pentagon figures.

Mr Trump said the conflict was not initiated by Washington, arguing instead that Tehran “has been waging war on America since 1979.”

He said US forces were acting to stop Iran from gaining the ability to build a nuclear weapon.

Speaking to troops, veterans and senior officials from his administration, Mr Trump singled out Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — who attended the ceremony — saying he had “done a fantastic job.”

Republicans in the US House of Representatives yesterday blocked an effort, introduced by an outgoing Republican lawmaker, to impeach Mr Hegseth over allegations that he waged war without congressional authorization and abused his authority as Pentagon chief.

Mr Trump, 80, also took part in a wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a revered site honouring US service members whose remains were never identified.

In his comments, he returned to his plan for a 250-foot-tall (76 metres) triumphal arch to be built just outside the cemetery, saying it would be dedicated “soon.”

Yesterday, the family of John F Kennedy asked a court to halt construction, saying the large structure would obstruct views and cast shadows over the gravesites of the slain president and other Kennedy family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

The proposed project is also facing lawsuits filed by a group of veterans, the city of Washington and the state of Virginia.

Cruise missiles fired at Riyadh

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis said it intercepted three cruise missiles fired toward Riyadh, which has been under weeks of attacks blamed on the Iran-backed group.

“Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 3 cruise missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area,” coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.

The interception was reported days after the Houthis damaged a skyscraper owned by oil giant Saudi Aramco in the capital’s financial district on Sunday.

Riyadh’s international airport has also come under repeated attack, with deadly strikes forcing it to shut down for two weeks last month.

Saudi Arabia formed an international coalition in 2015 to fight the Houthis after the group seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

After years of a fragile truce, the conflict flared again in July.

news.text:
A single aerial photo of the White House grounds has critics demanding the next president undo Trump's pet project.

Shannon Watts, founder of the gun safety group Moms Demand Action, offered a blunter verdict.

"Truly amazing," Glasser remarked.

news.title: Trump’s surprise judge pick blindsides GOP senators amid ‘power grab’: NYT
news.text:
A last-minute move by President Donald Trump to stack the federal bench has left even some of his Republican allies caught off guard.

Senate Republicans are scrambling to confirm as many as 25 of Trump's judicial nominees before Democrats take over the chamber in January, The New York Times reported Wednesday, and one of those picks was slipped onto the list for a Texas court without the usual sign-off from the state's two GOP senators.

That nominee, Elliot Gaiser, just stepped down from a senior post in the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel. Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) noted that Gaiser bypassed the screening process he and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) run for the state's judicial openings and said the two had sent the White House other qualified names for the Northern District seat.

"I will look at his record and make a decision," Cornyn said, adding that dropping in a nominee this late was unusual, a move he likened to an "airdrop."

The rush comes after Democrat James Talarico won a U.S. Senate seat in Texas last week. Once he is sworn in, longstanding Senate tradition will give him the power to block judicial picks for his home state, and Democrats have suggested the White House is hurrying to seat Gaiser and a second Texas nominee before that happens.

The other nominee, Texas Supreme Court Justice James Sullivan, lost his own bid for re-election last week.

"We are going to do our best to make sure that Talarico is not denied the basic right of a senator to decide whether a federal district court judge goes forward," said Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL), the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Durbin also dismissed Gaiser's ties to Texas as tangential and said the nominee had issued "unhinged" opinions during his time at the Justice Department. He accused Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-IA) of cutting corners by rushing hearings and shortchanging the review of nominees' paperwork, charges Grassley brushed aside.

The Judiciary Committee kicked off the push Tuesday by advancing four nominees to the floor. Aides cited by the Times said the full slate includes four appeals court picks and 21 district court nominees, enough to keep senators in Washington deep into December.

Democrats have limited tools to stop it. Judicial nominees no longer need 60 votes, and Republicans still hold a 53-47 majority, so district court picks can clear the floor in a single day. Appeals court nominees take longer, and Democrats have vowed to force procedural votes to drag the process out.

"We should spare no effort to stop judges who will be on the bench long after we are gone," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), a Judiciary Committee member. "I'm going to do everything I can to fight them."

Progressive groups are urging Democrats to dig in. Svante Myrick, president of People for the American Way, said in a statement, "The outgoing Republican majority has no mandate to use its final weeks in power to ram through even more extremist judicial nominees who will put loyalty to the thoroughly rejected MAGA agenda above all else. Democrats must do all they can to stop this power grab."

news.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces ouster vote amid spy and affair scandals
news.text: Nvidia's board is meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, as the world's dominant supplier of AI chips grapples with reports of two extramarital affairs involving its longtime leader.Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the board meeting.The meeting marks a sharp shift from Sunday, when Nvidia's board expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.Nvidia's stock slid more than 8% in extended trading after the Wall Street Journal first reported that the company was preparing to fire Huang. If those losses hold, Nvidia will have lost about $600 billion in market value since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang alleged to be a Chinese spy.Revelations that US intelligence was probing Alice Huang for facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms set off a series of events: Wall Street began raising questions about Nvidia's governance and Jensen Huang's personal conduct, the company's board launched an internal investigation and hired outside counsel, while lawmakers began to push for tighter curbs on chip exports to China."The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk," said Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares. "Losing Jensen would be a real blow."NO OBVIOUS SUCCESSORHuang's potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4 trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of chips at the center of the global AI boom and US-China technology rivalry.Huang, 63, has no obvious successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia's stock. He also has dozens of direct reports, underscoring the tight control he maintains over the company.Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that Nvidia's board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for Huang, citing a person familiar with the situation.Rosenberg said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who has held the role for more than a decade, would be the natural choice as an interim CEO, but said the bigger question was who would lead Nvidia's technology roadmap longer term.Odds on prediction market website Polymarket shifted sharply to show an 88% chance that Huang would resign or be removed by the end of the year. Odds for his successor favored Ian Buck, who oversees the business that serves Nvidia's data center clients.The leadership turmoil comes just days before investors are set to hear from the company on its financial performance and outlook, with its quarterly results due on November 17.Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him. The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five people who worked at the company.When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly." He then hung up, the New York Times reported.Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. news.title: Iran displays underground missiles and threatens wider US strikes
news.text:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) released images of tunnels containing ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, mobile launchers and military vehicles. The footage, circulated on Tuesday during the force’s Aerospace Week, showed senior commanders inspecting what Iranian authorities described as a new missile city.

Iran has not disclosed the facility’s location, dimensions or inventory. The images do not independently establish when the complex was built, how many weapons are operational or whether the systems shown could withstand another military campaign. Parts of the footage were obscured.

Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, and Brigadier General Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, appeared in the video touring the installation. Abdollahi warned that another attack on Iran would prompt a response extending beyond the region.

The warning was reinforced by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, who said American installations in European countries and distant locations could be targeted if they supported attacks on Iranian territory.

Rezaei told Al Mayadeen that Tehran would not restrict retaliation to American bases in neighbouring countries. He said military facilities from which US aircraft departed to bomb Iran could become targets, regardless of their distance from the Islamic Republic.

His remarks widened the geographical scope of Iran’s declared response, although Tehran provided no independently verifiable evidence that its missiles could reach every location mentioned. The statements were conditional threats rather than announcements of attacks already undertaken.

The footage also showed missiles mounted on transport vehicles and stored alongside launch equipment. Iranian military presentations identified the complex as part of the IRGC Aerospace Force’s infrastructure, but did not publish technical specifications or permit independent inspection of the installation.

Among the systems observers identified from the images were missiles resembling Iran’s Fattah and Khorramshahr families. Iran has described the Fattah as a hypersonic weapon, but the video offers no basis for verifying its performance, guidance characteristics or readiness for deployment.

IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohibbi had said ahead of the unveiling that missile and drone manufacturing operations were being transferred from exposed surface installations to protected underground facilities. He portrayed the move as an effort to preserve production capacity during aerial bombardment.

Mohibbi also said Iran had removed previous restrictions on missile range. Officials did not specify a revised maximum distance or provide testing evidence supporting an expansion of operational reach. Tehran had previously referred to a self-imposed range ceiling of approximately 2,000 kilometres.

The announcements follow months of confrontation involving Iran, the United States and Israel. American and Israeli attacks have targeted Iranian military infrastructure, while Tehran has sought to demonstrate that its missile forces remain capable of responding despite damage sustained during the fighting.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Iran was effectively defeated militarily, a characterisation at odds with Tehran’s public presentation of its remaining capabilities. Neither side has released a comprehensive, independently verified assessment of Iran’s surviving missile stockpiles or launch infrastructure.

Trump also indicated that renewed American air strikes were unlikely, while maintaining pressure on Tehran. The contrasting messages underscored the uncertainty surrounding the military standoff, with Iranian commanders stressing deterrence and Washington retaining the option of further operations.

Iranian officials have described underground storage and manufacturing as central to protecting missile assets from aerial surveillance and strikes. However, footage of weapons inside hardened tunnels cannot establish the facilities’ resilience, the availability of replacement components or the ability to sustain launches under attack.

The display came amid competing claims about the effectiveness of earlier strikes against Iran’s missile programme. Assessing those claims is difficult because the number of launchers destroyed, repaired or replaced has not been independently established. Underground facilities can conceal equipment and complicate targeting, but their existence does not demonstrate that missiles can be launched at the rate claimed by officials. Iran has supplied no inventory figures allowing comparisons with its arsenal before the fighting.

The video included Iranian flags, Revolutionary Guard insignia and military personnel accompanying the commanders through the passages. Some weapons and equipment were deliberately blurred, limiting identification of systems. Iranian authorities have not announced whether foreign observers will be allowed access to the site.

news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 12 (IANS) Democratic military veterans in Congress and newly elected colleagues called for an end to the Iran war, as their party used Veterans Day to press for stronger protections for service members and expanded access to veterans' healthcare. They pledged to seek an end to the conflict while pursuing lower costs, broader healthcare access and protections for military families. Separately, Senator Tammy Duckworth urged Congress to pass legislation extending protections for veterans exposed to toxic substances during the Iran war. Speaking on Veterans Day in Belleville, Illinois, the Illinois Democrat said her New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would address gaps that could prevent returning personnel from receiving care and benefits. The proposal would establish a presumption of toxic exposure for veterans who served in Iran, including its airspace and territorial waters, according to her office. It would also require periodic reviews of overseas assignments for toxic hazards and a review within 180 days when the military begins a contingency operation. "Because no servicemember should fight a war overseas only to come home and be faced with another battle to get the care they've rightfully earned through their service," Duckworth said. The measure remains proposed legislation. Her Veterans Day appeal sought congressional passage, rather than announcing that the additional protections had taken effect. The White House, meanwhile, highlighted President Donald Trump's pledge to support veterans during his appearance at Arlington National Cemetery. Its account quoted him promising that "while I'm President of the United States, we will always fulfil our duty to them."
