news.title: Trump's Veterans Day Message Compared to Those of Potential 2028 Contenders
news.text: President Donald Trump used his Veterans Day address at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday to honor U.S. service members while highlighting his administration's military record, veterans policies and foreign policy priorities. Trump praised the sacrifices of those who served in uniform and said Americans owed an enduring debt to veterans. "On Veterans Day, we honor those who have worn the uniform, who have worn the battle, who have stood to watch, whose ranks have formed the mighty wall of flesh and blood, of bravery and devotion that has defended our freedom for 250 years," Trump said. He pointed to record military recruiting numbers, improvements in veterans' care and America's renewed strength on the world stage as accomplishments of his administration. "Our republic has triumphed, and today our country is stronger than it has ever been before," Trump said. The president referenced U.S. operations involving Iran and Venezuela, argued that American military power had been restored under his leadership and contrasted his administration's handling of veterans' issues with that of previous administrations. He also touted his most recent construction project. “Soon, we’re going to dedicate a magnificent triumphal arch to our veterans,” Trump told the crowd at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Virginia. “And that’s in honor of our great veterans and our great military. They’ve been waiting for it for 200 years." Potential 2028 Republican Contenders Although the 2028 Republican presidential race has yet to take shape, Vice President JD Vance has consistently been viewed as an early front-runner in polling and prediction markets. Other Republicans frequently mentioned as potential contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis. This is not a comprehensive list. JD Vance Vance, who served in the U.S. Marine Corps from 2003 to 2007, recognized three World War II veterans alongside Trump at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday. “One of the most important things our veterans do is not just fight for their country; they fight for their fellow veterans," Vance told the crowd. "And let me say, as one veteran to the next, we are picking up that torch every single day. We will never leave our veterans behind.” Marco Rubio Rubio, who is in Paris for the G7 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, released a video message on One America News Network, urging Americans to care for military members and their families. "There is no higher calling for a citizen than defense of country, but in America today, it is a duty shouldered by less than 1 percent of our total population," he said in part. Ron DeSantis The term-limited governor of Florida is reportedly setting up a conservative think tank and considering whether to make a 2028 bid, after suspending his 2024 presidential run. He said service members should be honored for being willing to make the ultimate sacrifice for their country. "Anyone who puts on the cloth of our country is sacrificing for something bigger than any individual," the governor posted to X in part. Glenn Youngkin Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin, who has success in a state that has trended Democratic, is frequently mentioned as a potential Republican contender in early 2028 discussions. He marked Veterans Day by honoring the service and sacrifice of veterans and military families and expressing gratitude for their role in defending the nation's freedoms. "Our veterans represent the very best of America: courage, selfishness, patriotism, and an unwavering commitment to something greater than themselves, Youngkin posted to X in part. Potential 2028 Democratic Contenders Several Democrats who posted Veterans Day messages are frequently mentioned as potential 2028 presidential contenders. Prediction markets and early political speculation have focused on figures including former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, Georgia U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff and nearly a dozen others. Kamala Harris The former vice president and 2024 Democratic nominee has said she is "thinking about" a 2028 presidential campaign but has not decided. Harris sent a message on X Wednesday, thanking veterans and their families. "They represent the best of who we are as Americans," she wrote in part. Gavin Newsom The governor of California paired his Veterans Day tribute with a policy-focused message, arguing that honoring veterans requires providing housing, healthcare and economic opportunities for those who have served and their families. While Newsom has not announced a 2028 presidential campaign, he is widely viewed as a potential contender after years of building a national profile as one of the Democratic Party's most prominent voices. On X, in part, the governor honored "the extraordinary men and women who answered the call to serve our country." Josh Shapiro The Pennsylvania governor, also widely viewed as a potential Democratic presidential contender, has frequently appeared near the top of early 2028 polling and speculation about the party's future leadership. Shapiro marked Veterans Day with a personal tribute to his father, a Navy veteran, thanking him and other veterans for protecting American freedoms at home and abroad. "Nearly 700,000 veterans call Pennsylvania home — brave men and women who put on the uniform and served our Commonwealth and our country. On behalf of all of us, thank you for the countless sacrifices you made to fight for our freedoms and defend the values of our nation," the governor posted to X, in part. Pete Buttigieg The former transportation secretary, who previously sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020 and remains a frequent subject of 2028 speculation, has continued to appear in early polling and discussions about the party's next generation of national leaders. Buttigieg, a Navy Reserve veteran who deployed to Afghanistan, marked Veterans Day by honoring service members and veterans while reflecting on the sacrifices made by military families and those who have worn the uniform. "Without their courage, our way of life would be nothing but a pleasant theory," he said on X, in part. Jon Ossoff The U.S. senator from Georgia who won reelection last week also appears near the top of early 2028 polling on the Democratic Party's future leadership. "Veterans Day is not a day for sales at the mall. It's a day for us to reflect on our shared debt to those who have worn the uniform and served our nation and to their families," Ossoff said in a message shown on YouTube. "We are Americans first before we are Democrats or Republicans." Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Ocasio-Cortez, whose name has also regularly surfaced in speculation about the Democratic Party's future leadership, honored veterans and military families in a message marking their service and sacrifice. She says the government owes its veterans more. "This Veterans Day, we must move past words and pass legislation to guarantee robust benefits for all who have served," the New York Democrat posted to X, in part. news.title: ‘Shouting match’, Trump, Netanyahu clash over future of Iran war: Report
news.text: United States President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu engaged in a heated telephone conversation over the preceding days, which reportedly deteriorated into an acrimonious exchange amid ongoing disagreements regarding the course of the war with Iran, according to Israeli media reports.According to reports from Israeli news organisations Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, the Israeli leader repeatedly pushed for renewed military action, whereas the American President preferred allowing ongoing peace negotiations with Tehran to continue.Netanyahu has consistently argued that Washington should resume strikes and actively pursue regime change within the Islamic Republic, while Trump has favoured maintaining economic pressure to secure diplomatic concessions from Tehran. The Israeli Prime Minister's Office rejected claims that the conversation became confrontational, describing the reports as "fake news".Israeli news outlets Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Netanyahu repeatedly urged Trump to restart the war during the call. Trump, however, continued to back a diplomatic approach as talks with Iran progressed.Sources quoted by both outlets described the conversation as having descended into a "shouting match from hell". A senior Israeli official confirmed that the two leaders spoke over the weekend but denied that any confrontation had taken place.Trump and Netanyahu have previously had heated telephone exchanges over the conflict. Following several disagreements in June, Trump told The Post that he had called Netanyahu "f***ing crazy" during one conversation.The latest reports emerged days after the Financial Times said Netanyahu had been telephoning Trump daily to persuade him to resume an all-out war. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, is facing uncertainty over his position after losing seats in the general election held in October.Netanyahu has continued to argue that Washington must restart attacks on Iran and pursue regime change. Addressing the 26th Knesset assembly on Tuesday, he said replacing Iran's leadership was the only way to end what he described as Tehran's reign of terror and halt its nuclear programme.“Iran is working to renew the nuclear threat. The only way to permanently remove this existential threat is by toppling the ayatollah regime,” Netanyahu said.Trump has resisted calls to resume the conflict, choosing instead to let the US economic pressure campaign continue in an effort to compel Iran to make concessions. Asked during a "60 Minutes" interview on Sunday whether he would restart the war, Trump said he did not think "there's any reason to".The reported exchange underscored the leaders' differing positions, with Netanyahu seeking renewed military action and regime change in Iran, while Trump continued to favour diplomacy and economic pressure. Israel has denied that the weekend call developed into a clash.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly clashed over the war with Iran during a tense weekend phone call. Netanyahu pushed for renewed military action and regime change, while Trump favoured ongoing peace talks and economic pressure. Israel denied the confrontation occurred.

news.title: US midterms put pro-Israel AIPAC on defensive
news.text:
WASHINGTON: For years, the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC was a US political juggernaut, but deepening voter disillusion over US-Israeli ties and wins by openly Israel-sceptic candidates in last week’s midterm elections have left it reeling.

Candidates of all stripes long courted the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s support. But what was once an asset has become a liability in many races, as favourable opinions of Israel plummet over civilian deaths in Gaza and the costly Iran war.

In the Michigan Senate race, AIPAC’s once irresistible force ran into an immovable object. Demo-crat Abdul El-Sayed — who tapped into anger over US funding for Israel’s military — faced AIPAC-supported candidates in both the primary and general election, but emerged victorious to become the first Muslim senator.

The tens of millions of dollars spent by an AIPAC-affiliated group, the United Democracy Project, not only failed to beat El-Sayed — they helped him boost his own messaging. “To AIPAC… Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice,” the Michigan politician taunted in his victory speech.

The tables flipped so completely that allies of El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, reportedly even asked the group to stop spending on him at one point. “They definitely have become a liability,” Adam Wood, a veteran Democratic campaign strategist with City & State Public Affairs, said, noting several campaigns he worked on in years past “coveted” AIPAC’s support.

Another Democratic Senate success story, James Talarico, won in Texas with a similar message of ending US funding for Israeli offensive weaponry and keeping distance from AIPAC. “I’ve never taken money from AIPAC, and I’m not taking money from AIPAC in this campaign,” Talarico said early in his bid.

Israel support plummets

Officially, AIPAC is nonpartisan. It has traditionally supported candidates from both the left and the right.

According to its website, it only accepts money from Americans and its board is composed exclusively of Americans. But the group has become a byword in US politics for Washington’s tight ties with Israeli governments, including the outgoing far-right coalition of Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Chicago Council on Global Affairs has asked Americans to rate their favourability of Israel on a scale of 0 to 100 regularly since 1978 and this year marked a record low: an average score of just 44.

That’s down from 58 in 2022, when the previous midterms were held. And for Democrats, the numbers are all the starker: a drop in favourability from 52 in 2022 to just 30 today.

“Democrats started to really tank on Israel,” Dina Smeltz, a former State Department official who is now a managing director at the council, said.

Leftist Democratic star, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has branded AIPAC as “a right-wing organization that undermines democracy.” But support also appears to be faltering on the right.

On election day, President Donald Trump dialed into his favorite morning program, Fox & Friends, and made the surprising announcement that the US would be ending a major annual aid package to Israel — something El-Sayed and others on the left have repeatedly demanded.

Vice President JD Vance said he’d been told by a trusted pollster that his party’s road to recovery after the midterms annihilation will require, in part, changing “our relationship to Israel.” And other right-wing voices, including broadcaster Tucker Carlson and libertarian Representative Thomas Massie, have openly criticized Israel in recent years in ways unimaginable in the 2000s and 2010s.

Pro-Israel lobbyists are not going to go away of course. AIPAC already has competition from the left-leaning pro-Israel J Street as well as the recently formed pro-Palestine American Priorities super PAC.

The aftermath of elections in Israel, with the possible political eclipse of Netanyahu, could also help AIPAC to find its feet again. “It has been around for a long time, it has a lot of money,” Smeltz said.

news.title: Nvidia may fire Jensen Huang over ‘double affair’ with alleged spy and executive
news.text: Nvidia’s board is preparing to remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, The Wall Street Journal reports, three days after the same board said it trusted his leadership. The move follows Huang’s admission that he had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials believe works for China’s spy services. According to WSJ, Huang also had a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, the senior Nvidia executive who runs the company’s healthcare business.The board was planning to meet as soon as Wednesday to decide his future, WSJ reported. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and built a gaming chip startup into the AI industry’s main chip supplier, with an estimated 90% share of that market. Nvidia shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading on the news.Nvidia board backed Jensen Huang just days before the ouster reportOn November 8, Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. At the time, it said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is running the probe.The same day, Huang admitted the affair in a letter to employees and apologised to his family. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy,” he wrote.Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Its Malaysian sister company bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia-powered equipment between June 2024 and February 2026. US officials suspect Megaspeed of diverting some of those chips to China. A Commerce Department probe into the firm began in late 2024 and has since moved to the Justice Department, which WSJ says is now leading multiple investigations involving her. China has denied the espionage claims, and Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment.Kimberly Powell relationship puts Nvidia’s own conduct rules in focusPowell, 48, joined Nvidia in 2008 and has headed its healthcare unit since late 2017. People who worked at the company say the relationship was discussed internally. Two of them said the pair were filmed being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia’s GTC conference in March. Huang’s security team then had the bystander who filmed them sign a non-disclosure agreement. Both are married to other people.Nvidia’s code of conduct asks employees to avoid conflicts that arise from personal relationships. Asked about Powell over the phone, Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” and hung up. Powell has not commented.Boards have acted on this before. Intel’s Brian Krzanich resigned in 2018 over a past relationship with an employee, and McDonald’s removed Steve Easterbrook a year later for similar breaches.Nvidia has no succession plan for Jensen HuangThe harder question for the board is who comes next. Huang, 63, has around 60 direct reports and has said he doesn’t believe in succession planning. He is also Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, with a stake of about 3.56%. The company’s own proxy statement warns that Nvidia is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team.” WSJ notes there is no clear successor.Pressure is building outside Nvidia too. Republican leaders of three House committees have asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on his dealings with Alice Huang. A class-action shareholder lawsuit was also filed on Monday in a California federal court.President Donald Trump was briefed on the intelligence about a year ago and took no action. He has stood by Huang, calling him an “amazing guy” and an “honorable man” who did not know she was a suspected spy.On Sunday, the board said it trusted Huang to lead. By Wednesday, it was deciding whether Nvidia, a company he has run for 33 years, can carry on without him.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang, WSJ reports, days after backing his leadership. Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive US officials suspect is a Chinese spy, and reportedly had a second relationship with Nvidia healthcare VP Kimberly Powell. The board was set to meet as soon as Wednesday to decide the co-founder’s future, with no clear succession plan in place.

news.title: Democrat Scott Colom Becomes Mississippi’s First Black US Senator Since 1874
news.text: Jackson [Mississippi]: Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's United States Senate race, securing a historic victory that makes him the first Black senator from the Southern state in more than 150 years, according to media projections.Colom's landmark win marks the first time since the Reconstruction era following the American Civil War that Mississippi has elected a Black representative to the upper chamber. The previous Black candidate to achieve this feat was former slave Blanche Bruce in 1874.The outcome carries immense significance in a traditionally conservative state where President Donald Trump secured a victory by nearly 23 percentage points during the 2024 presidential election and actively campaigned for Hyde-Smith in the final stages of the campaign.The Mississippi contest was among the final uncalled races stemming from the November 3 midterm elections. Vote counting continued for more than a week amid an exceptionally tight race, during which Colom held leads of just dozens of votes before final media projections established a margin of more than 4,500 votes, representing roughly 0.5 percentage points.The 43-year-old district attorney also became the first Democrat to claim a Mississippi Senate seat since John Stennis in 1982.The breakthrough further strengthens the congressional majority held by Democrats following widespread gains in the midterms that stripped Republicans of control of both legislative chambers.The Mississippi outcome establishes a 55-44 Democratic advantage in the 100-member Senate, while one race in Alaska remains unresolved. In the House of Representatives, Democrats have picked up 41 seats to secure a 254-168 advantage, with 13 contests still awaiting final projections.Consequently, losing control of both chambers leaves President Trump facing a Democratic-led legislative branch for the first time during his presidential tenures, granting the opposition greater leverage to block partisan measures and initiate inquiries into executive governance.Hyde-Smith, 67, was elected to office in 2018 and had maintained consistent leads in pre-election polling across a traditionally conservative electorate, further bolstered by President Trump's late campaign rally.Conversely, Colom's campaign gained momentum from October rallies featuring Democratic Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Cory Booker of New Jersey.The rivalry also featured past political friction between the contenders. In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination by then-President Joe Biden for a federal judgeship in northern Mississippi, citing his positions on transgender issues, although Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker, had supported the nomination.

news.title: Engulfed by scandals, AI chip powerhouse Nvidia's CEO Huang facing ouster: Reports
news.text: Digital Desk | New York, Nov 12 (IANS) Engulfed by scandals, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are a driving force in the AI revolution, is facing ouster by the company's board, a development with far-reaching consequences for the US economy and its technological leadership. The board was meeting Wednesday evening (local time in the US) to decide on the fate of Huang, who has admitted to an affair with a woman who is suspected of being a spy for China, and was reported to be involved with another woman working for him, according to several independent news reports. In what could be a classic honeypot spy trap involving Alice Le Huang (not related to him despite the shared surname), the scandal reaches into the highest levels of technology, business and government. The upheaval comes as President Donald Trump prepares to go to China for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit next week, where he will meet with President Xi Jinping. China has denied any intelligence links to Alice Huang. Huang was closely identified with President Donald Trump, who loosened the ban on selling high-end chips to China by allowing him to sell a second-level chip to Beijing with a cut for the government. Huang had lobbied for selling advanced chips to China, opposing the US ban to keep China from catching up with it in the AI race. Trump gave him a clean chit on Monday, telling reporters, "I just know Jensen very well; I just think he's a very honourable man." The scandal comes on the heels of the Republican Party rout in the midterm elections, and the party itself has called Huang for a closed-door briefing with the House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee and threatened him with a subpoena if he does not come. When the Democrats take over Congress next year, he and his links in the US and abroad will come in for greater scrutiny. Huang built Nvidia from a chipmaker for gaming computers to the lynchpin of the AI revolution, powering virtually all major Western AI companies and helping keep the US lead in the domain. The danger to US AI dominance is that Huang kept an iron-fisted control over the company without a hierarchy or an obvious successor to him, and that could cloud the company's future. About 60 department heads reported directly to him, and a successor would have to not only wield the same level of control but also be knowledgeable enough and capable of continuing the company's pioneering work. The company stock fell from its peak of $243.37 on October 6 to $158.78 in after-hours trading on Wednesday, a decline of nearly 35 per cent, and acting as a drag on many indexes. Nvidia was the richest US company by value but, as the scandal unravelled, conceded that position to Apple, while Huang slipped from the sixth position on the Forbes billionaire ranking to 12th with a net worth of about $148 billion on Wednesday. A succession crisis would have an economic impact across the AI sector because of the reliance on Nvidia chips, and beyond. The AI sector has been an important driver of the stock market boom. Anthropic, one of the giants of AI that rides on Nvidia chips and is preparing to go public, has valued itself at as much as $1.46 trillion. Any disruption could have wider repercussions that reach into the retirement funds of millions in the US. Even if China had not received any trade secrets through Alice Huang, it could still benefit from any upheaval in the US AI sector due to the fallout of the scandal. The New York Times reported on Wednesday (local time) Huang's alleged affair with a company executive, Kimberly Powell, who is the vice president of health care, in violation of the company code of conduct, adding to his travails. Huang, 68, is married for 41 years to Lori Huang, whom he met while they were engineering students, and made a public apology to her for the affair with the Chinese woman. Besides the possibility of company secrets, that affair drew scrutiny because of fears that Alice Huang had diverted advanced chips to China. She was an executive with a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that the Times reported was a shell outfit used to buy the advanced chips and divert them to China or use them through Southeast Asia companies. She had worked as a TV reporter before getting into banking on her way to entrepreneurship with Megaspeed. Media reports said that several months ago US intelligence agencies had raised suspicions about her links to China's Ministry of State Security, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had warned Trump about it. Trump has asserted that he did not receive it. Huang was not on the list of US business leaders to accompany Trump to China during his May visit, perhaps because of the doubts about him, But Trump, who learned about it after the trip had started, arranged for Huang to meet Air Force One during a refuelling stop in Alaska and join him on board.

news.title: White House confronts Democrats over planned probes, claiming possible ‘criminality’
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to “blatant criminality.”

White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to “lawyer up” as his party was on the way to stunning victories in last week’s midterm election.

In response, Scharf wrote that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.” The letter’s existence was first reported by Punchbowl News.

It’s just the latest shot across the bow as the White House prepares to square off against newly empowered Democrats in the House and Senate next year, a showdown with major implications for congressional authority and the balance of power between the branches of government.

Garcia pushes back on the White House letter

Outside the Capitol on Wednesday, Garcia told reporters that “Donald Trump is clearly hiding something” and that Democrats “are not going to be threatened or intimidated.”

“The truth is that he needs to understand that Congress is a coequal branch of government,” Garcia said.

He doubled down on his “lawyer up” post after the election, saying the White House was “thin-skinned” and couldn’t “take any sort of heat.”

“If you have abused the American public, you should lawyer up,” Garcia said. “If you’re a corporate CEO and you’re ripping off the American people, you should lawyer up.”

Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing.

Garcia also wants to look at the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. Other targets include Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals and Trump’s crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff.

The Republican chair of Oversight says the panel is ‘very independent’

Kentucky Republican James Comer, the current chair of the Oversight Committee who conducted a wide-ranging investigation of former President Joe Biden and his family, told The Associated Press on Wednesday that he had not yet read the letter from the White House, but stressed that the panel is “very independent.”

“Regardless of who is in the White House, there’s always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch, regardless of the political scenario,” Comer said.

He said he thought Garcia’s “lawyer up” comments were in “bad taste” but Democrats “won the election and it’s going to be his committee. So if he gets out of line, I would assume that his members will try to rein him in.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that “there could be” a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying “Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it’s through subpoenas or letters — so we’re not going to stop working with Congress.”

“Nothing I’ve said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise,” he added.

Still, Justice Department officials elsewhere were pushing back. Aaron Reitz, the US attorney in the Southern District of Texas, wrote to Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal on Wednesday, telling him to preserve all records relevant to his investigations.

Blumenthal is poised to chair a powerful Senate investigative committee in January. Reitz called Blumenthal’s efforts an “intent to deprive citizens of their core constitutional rights,” pointing to his October letter to people who donated to the new White House ballroom.

In response, Blumenthal said he “will not be intimidated.”

“The Trump administration is so afraid of transparency and oversight that they are weaponizing the Department of Justice to baselessly target Congress in direct violation of the Constitution,” he said in a statement.

Other lawmakers react to the White House’s warning

Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, said he hopes Democrats don’t squander their new powers on “stupid things.”

“I hope they have real hearings about real things, not another Russia-gate,” he said, referring to a previous congressional inquiry into ties between Trump’s first presidential campaign in 2016 and Russia. Trump repeatedly denounced that investigation as a “hoax.”

“I think there is some real corruption there around the fringes,” Massie said about Trump and some of those around the president. Massie lost his primary election to a Trump-backed GOP challenger.

Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., who is expected to be the next House Ethics Committee chairman, said he would not back down from any investigations because of warnings from the White House.

“If they’re trying to intimidate, at least for me, it’s not going to get me,” said DeSaulnier, who was a Republican before he switched to the Democratic Party in 2000. “I don’t work for a mafia, a mob organization.”

news.text:
You may have thought it was a headline from the Babylon Bee: Hunter Biden Honored for “Outstanding Contribution to Public Discourse” from prestigious Trinity College Dublin. 

But it was true. 

Hunter Biden, the 56-year-old reformed crack and prostitute connoisseur of “Laptop from Hell” fame, visited his ancestral land to be so honored on Tuesday, accompanied by his suddenly compos mentis father, Joe, the former president. 

A Secret Service cavalcade of seven vehicles chauffeured Hunter and Joe to the university from Dublin’s finest five-star luxury Merrion hotel. 

We were told that Joe wiped tears from his eyes as his son, fully dressed, accepted Trinity’s gold medal for contributions to society amid glowing accolades from Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, who posted photos of their meeting on social media. 

Jesus wept. 

You will be seeing a lot more such gaslighting historical rewrites in coming weeks as Joe’s latest memoir, “Promise Me, America,” is published next Tuesday. 

You have to hand it to wily old Joe: the 83-year-old still knows how to garner positive press coverage. Unlike President Trump, he confines his utterances to gushingly friendly media, like People magazine, even when he’s supposed to be selling a book for which he received a $10 million advance.

‘I wasn’t hiding’

“I’m not saying I’ll live forever but the point is that I have all my faculties.” 

See how smoothly he wipes away the memory of the cognitive impairment that we all saw accelerate throughout his presidency.

Joe would never lie.

People happened to be at the Biden family’s “lake house” compound in Greenville, Del., two days after the midterm election. 

Joe was happy as Larry.

Jill was cock-a-hoop about the election result thrilled, too. She loves James Talarico. 

“I do think, when history is written, the true story . . . of all [Joe’s] years in office [will be told],” she said, “and people will realize, not just what a great president he was, but what a great man he is.” 

Bold hypocrisy 

Only if the Bidens brainwash all the historians, which is, of course, why Joe gathered so many pet leftist historical authors around him for intimate gatherings at the White House. Jon Meacham, Doris Kearns Goodwin and Michael Beschloss were among those who murmured sweet nothings in Joe’s ear and told him he was the second coming of FDR. 

But history will have a very different take on Biden’s legacy, no matter how many lies are spun in this latest attempt to gloss his failed presidency. 

Take his beef that Trump reversed the “successful policies pursued by my administration.” 

In a book extract published this week by The Atlantic, Biden says the reversals happened because of the “dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.” 

This is hypocrisy so dishonest it takes your breath away. 

Maybe Biden has forgotten who his predecessor was. Trump!

In his first 100 days, Biden signed more than 60 executive actions, of which 24 were “direct reversals of Trump policies,” CNN reported. Ten of his first 12 executive orders reversed Trump immigration measures.

He maliciously locked up hundreds of non-violent Trump supporters without trial over Jan. 6 and maligned half the country as “semi-fascist ultra-MAGA” in a series of angry, ranting speeches we have tried to forget. 

“The last president of the United States issued executive orders I felt were very counterproductive to our security, counterproductive to who we are as a country, particularly in the area of immigration,” Biden declared on Feb. 2, 2021, as he signed the orders in the Oval Office and flung open the border to all comers. 

The facts are clear 

The rest is catastrophic history that can never be unwritten: the largest border invasion in US history — as many as 25 million illegal aliens, mainly from the Third World, unvetted on criminal, terrorist or character grounds. 

Left-wing nonprofits then set about registering them to vote for absolutely no reason at all, since Democrats constantly assure us there is no way these non-citizens would vote because that would be illegal.

He also presided over a 21% increase in prices over his term, thanks to flagrant government spending, that can never be undone, not to mention a turbocharging of welfare fraud.

Clearly, Biden thinks he would have won the 2024 election, slyly slipping a claim into his memoir that Trump told him when they met in the Oval Office for the last time “that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me.” 

Sure thing, Corn Pop.

news.title: Trump blamed for ‘punching holes’ in red wall as MAGA bastion falls in stunning upset: WSJ
news.text:
A former Republican leader in one of the GOP's most storied strongholds is laying a stunning defeat at the feet of one man.

Nathan Leupp, a Bob Jones University alumnus and former chair of the Greenville County Republican Party in South Carolina, told The Wall Street Journal in a report published Wednesday that President Donald Trump bears much of the blame after Democrat Annie Andrews captured the Senate seat Lindsey Graham held for more than two decades. Andrews not only won statewide but also carried Greenville County, a conservative bastion Trump won by 22 points in 2024.

"I fully believe that South Carolina would have been the only red wall for that blue wave except for Lindsey Graham's passing and President Trump personally punching holes through our red wall by selecting our nominee," Leupp said.

Graham died in July, and Trump threw his weight behind the late senator's sister, Darline Graham, a first-time candidate The Journal described as untested and hesitant. According to the report, the president's anointing rubbed many independent-minded South Carolinians the wrong way.

The upheaval scrambled the calendar too. After a second primary in August, Graham beat Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) in a runoff two weeks later and limped into the general election broke. Andrews went on to outraise her $24 million to $2 million while the county GOP stayed mired in infighting between MAGA loyalists and the party's old guard.

Some conservatives rejected Trump's claim that he was not on the ballot. Steve Pettit, a former Bob Jones University president who now leads the socially conservative Palmetto Family Council, called the result "really a response to the president." Randy Page, a longtime South Carolina political operative, put it more bluntly.

"Yes, he was," Page insisted.

Page added that Trump's three campaign stops for Graham were a red flag in themselves.

"Any time a Republican president is coming to South Carolina during a general election, it means one thing," he said. "You're losing."

Former Republican Gov. David Beasley, who accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020 as head of the United Nations World Food Program, cut a joint ad backing Andrews with Jim Hodges, the Democrat who unseated him in 1998. Beasley told The Journal he was outraged when Trump called Andrews "Annie Trannie" and no longer considers himself a Republican.

"That party we built?" Beasley said. "That party doesn't exist anymore."

news.title: Trump handed yet another midterms blow as Democrats win Mississippi senator for first time in decades
news.text: Donald Trump has been given another midterms blow after the Democrats pulled off a stunning upset in Mississippi. Scott Colom is the first Democratic Senator in the state since the 1940s. Colom, a prosecutor, defeated Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday (November 11) in Mississippi’s closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi. It has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations, despite having the largest share of black residents of any US state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump , whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states like Texas and Georgia, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South. Ms Hyde-Smith was magnanimous in defeat. The 67-year-old said in a two-minute concession speech posted online: “While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.” A spokesman for the senator said she called Colom to congratulate him and concede before the video was shared publicly. Colom scheduled a victory celebration with supporters Wednesday night in Jackson. The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947, and the winner then was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalized on the large black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term. “They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign’s closing stretch. Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society. “It’s got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better,” he added.

news.title: Trump is 'his own worst enemy' on judges — 'and so much else': WSJ
news.text:
President Donald Trump and his Republican supporters have long desired to stack America's courts with right-wing judges, an agenda that exists somewhat uncomfortably next to Trump's repeated alienation of those same judges. Now a conservative publication is arguing that Trump failed to realize the potential for a drastic Republican reshaping of the judiciary.

"On judges as on so much else, Mr. Trump is his own worst enemy," wrote The Wall Street Journal's Editorial Board on Wednesday. The publication observed that "one disappointment of President Trump’s second term is the relatively fewer judicial confirmations. With his nominees about to hit a brick wall next year, Republicans can make up some of the lost time by moving as many judges as possible in the lame-duck session."

They added, "Since January 2025, the Senate has confirmed 56 judicial nominees, including 10 for circuit courts, 45 for district courts and one to the Court of International Trade. In the same period in Mr. Trump’s first term, the Senate confirmed 84 judges, including 29 circuit judges, 53 district judges and Supreme Court Justices Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh. Senate Democrats confirmed 84 judges in Joe Biden’s corresponding time frame."

The publication concluded, "The judiciary is a major part of any President’s legacy, and the shame is that the GOP rout last week will cut short Mr. Trump’s opportunity. Only nominees who pass ideological approval by Democrats will be confirmed for the next two years. Mark it down as another result of the many White House mistakes that cost GOP control of the Senate."

In August, Judge John J. McConnell Jr., the Chief Justice of the United States District Court for the District of Rhode Island, told MS NOW’s Nicolle Wallace that Trump's attacks on the judiciary have negatively impacted the judges.

“It's not an easy thing for any of us to come forward and talk about the personal threats," McConnell told Wallace. "It's also not an easy thing for us to come forward as judges, because you all work on[.] There is an unprecedented amount of personal attacks against judges — not just me, but all across the country. It's systematic, it's growing, it's severe. There are sustained efforts.”

He added, “There are, in my opinion, results of sustained efforts by high-level members of the executive branch who have called judges rogue, insurrectionists, radicals, haters, moneyed, lunatics, corrupt, vicious. And this constant personal attack on my fellow district judges and myself and our families is the beginning of the attack on equal justice under the law, according to the rule of law.”

He continued, “My story is not unique — it's disturbing, but it's not unique. I received six or seven credible death threats. My daughter was doxxed by Laura Loomer and by Elon Musk. I have a picture of myself on a wanted poster made by a congressman. Ethics complaints were filed against me, and some of the attacks were against my wife — certainly not a public figure. And so that level of personally attacking judges by a co-equal branch of government is detrimental to our democracy as we know it.”

news.title: Trump and Netanyahu in Reported ‘Shouting Match’ Over Resuming Full-Scale War With Iran
news.text:
Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly engaged in what sources described as a “shouting match from hell” over how to proceed with the war in Iran.

Relations between the US president and Israeli prime minister have repeatedly become strained as the conflict has continued, despite Trump’s unwavering public support for Israel.

According to Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, the two leaders clashed over the weekend after Netanyahu pressed for military action to resume while Trump continued to favor negotiations aimed at securing peace.

In an interview with CBS News’ 60 Minutes on Sunday, Trump said he had no desire to restart the strikes.

“Well, I’m not looking to. I don’t think there’s any reason to. I don’t think there’s any reason to,” he said.

Sources familiar with the conversation said the pair launched into an explosive phone exchange.

Netanyahu’s representatives angrily rejected the account, dismissing it as “fake news, complete nonsense.”

A senior Israeli official likewise said the call was “very much not a difficult conversation.”

The Daily Mail has contacted the White House for comment.

The reported confrontation comes as both leaders face growing uncertainty over their political futures.

Trump’s Republican Party is expected to lose control of Congress in January after what has been dubbed a “blue tsunami” in the midterm elections. Netanyahu, meanwhile, remains well short of the majority required to retain the premiership following Israel’s elections.

It was not the first reported dispute between the two leaders since they began a joint military operation against Iran.

In May, Trump and Netanyahu reportedly argued over whether to attack Iran during a “dramatic” overnight phone call, shortly after details emerged of an unsuccessful effort to topple Tehran’s regime at the beginning of the war.

Israel’s Channel 12 described that conversation as “lengthy and dramatic.”

Weeks later, reports emerged that Trump had called Netanyahu “f***ing crazy” in a phone conversation shortly before announcing a pause in fighting between Israel and Hezbollah.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the Israeli prime minister had “turned his troops around” rather than carrying out a “major raid” in Lebanon on Monday.

He said the Israeli military and Hezbollah-linked militia groups had both agreed to “stop shooting” at one another.

Trump nevertheless offered a cautious response, writing: “Let’s see how long that lasts — Hopefully it will be for ETERNITY!”

Before that statement, the two leaders had reportedly exchanged tense words during a phone call about escalating violence in Lebanon involving Israel and Hezbollah.

According to a source cited by Axios, Trump at one point asked Netanyahu bluntly: “What the f*** are you doing?”

Trump then reportedly berated the prime minister, telling him that he would be in jail without US support.

“You’re f***ing crazy. You’d be in prison if it weren’t for me. I’m saving your ass. Everybody hates you now. Everybody hates Israel because of this,” he allegedly said.

Two sources told Axios that Trump accused Netanyahu of showing little gratitude and warned that following through on threats to bomb Beirut would further damage Israel’s position.

The sources suggested Trump believed Israel’s military actions were undermining efforts to negotiate a peace agreement with Iran.

Netanyahu later appeared to question Trump’s announcement of a ceasefire, warning that Israel would strike Beirut if Hezbollah continued attacking the country.

In June, Trump again claimed that “there would be no Israel” without him, while criticizing Netanyahu and accusing him of having “no f*****g judgment” during the Lebanon conflict.

Speaking to reporters at the G7 summit in France, Trump said Israel’s war with Hezbollah had gone on too long and urged Netanyahu to act more responsibly in Lebanon.

“Israel’s fighting Hezbollah too long and too many people are being killed,” he said during a bilateral meeting with Qatar’s emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani.

“You don’t have to knock down an apartment house every time you’re looking for somebody, because there are a lot of people in those apartment houses, and they’re not all Hezbollah, that I can tell you.”

Several weeks later, Trump criticized Netanyahu again before pledging to destroy Iran’s final nuclear facility, which is located deep inside a mountain.

The president rebuked the Israeli leader after Netanyahu told reporters he would provide Trump with evidence that Iran was continuing to develop its nuclear program at the site, known as Pickaxe Mountain.

“Well, I don’t need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved,” Trump told Fox News before meeting Netanyahu in the Oval Office.

Trump also cautioned Netanyahu against airing disagreements publicly, saying they should be discussed privately.

“I heard Bibi announce that. I said, ‘Why didn’t you just tell it to me? Why do you have to announce it to the world?’”

Despite the earlier disputes, the two appeared to have developed a more cordial relationship in recent months, with Trump taking credit for strengthening Netanyahu’s position ahead of the election.

Trump wrote: “When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a great prime minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu.”

On October 18, nine days before Israelis went to the polls, Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu and gave the country’s longest-serving prime minister his “complete and total endorsement.”

Netanyahu’s political future nevertheless remains uncertain after Israeli President Isaac Herzog asked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government.

Trump has also said the United States will end its financial aid to Israel by the close of the year following an agreement with Netanyahu.

“They don’t need it. Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an [Abdul] El-Sayed when they don’t need it? They no longer need it, Israel is a thriving country,” Trump said in a Tuesday interview with Fox & Friends.

He added: “Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping.”

Trump said the aid would be “cut off at the end of the year,” while leaving open the possibility that Washington could provide assistance again if circumstances changed.

“Now we’ll help Israel if they need it. You know they’ve been a great ally,” he said.

Trump also said Netanyahu understood that US aid to Israel had become a political target for Democrats, including Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a prominent critic of Israel.

“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” the president said.

“And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.”

Although the annual $4 billion in aid is set to end, the United States will continue selling weapons to Israel.

news.title: Democrats accuse US envoys of weakening Ukraine
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 12 (IANS) Three senior congressional Democrats have accused President Donald Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff of weakening Ukraine's negotiating position and undermining NATO, urging the President to reject concessions they said would benefit Russia. In a joint statement issued Wednesday (local time), Representatives Gregory Meeks and Adam Smith, together with Senator Jack Reed, challenged the envoys' approach to territorial questions and wider European security arrangements. Meeks is the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Smith and Reed hold the corresponding positions on the House and Senate Armed Services committees. The lawmakers alleged that the envoys were pressing Kyiv to surrender sovereign territory, including defensive positions that help prevent Russian forces from advancing westward. They also criticised discussions about reshaping European security and potentially reducing the Western military presence in Eastern Europe. "Their parroting of Kremlin talking points on renegotiating European security and possibly pulling back from Eastern Europe is totally unacceptable to the continued viability of NATO and the national security of the United States," they said. An official statement issued a day earlier following consultations involving the United States, Ukraine, European partners and NATO set out a different description of the diplomatic effort. Published by the Council of the European Union, that statement said participants agreed that future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity and independent decision-making, while providing credible security guarantees for Ukraine. It also said participants were clear that a strong NATO would remain central to collective defence across the Euro-Atlantic region. The consultations in Abu Dhabi brought together representatives of the EU, France, Germany, Italy, Britain, Ukraine, the United States and NATO ahead of trilateral discussions with Russia. Participants said they would continue coordinating throughout the negotiations and work towards broader talks involving European partners. In their statement, Meeks, Smith and Reed alleged that Kushner and Witkoff had repeatedly bypassed or undercut the US intelligence community and State Department. They argued that reducing pressure on Moscow while seeking concessions from Kyiv would not produce a durable settlement. They also said congressional support for Ukraine and NATO reflected American national interests. The lawmakers called on Trump to intervene directly. "The President should inform Kushner and Witkoff that surrendering in Ukraine and appeasing Putin will result in neither peace nor strength," they said. Their statement challenged both the substance of possible concessions and the way the administration was conducting diplomacy. Preparations for the talks included a November 4 telephone conversation between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the two US envoys. Ukraine said that the discussion covered the proposed trilateral format, air defence and bilateral cooperation. news.title: Fifty heads of state gather in Dublin for major European summit
news.text:
Fifty heads of state are gathering in the Irish capital to discuss the war in Ukraine and other major issues.

The biggest security operation in the history of the Irish state has been mounted in Dublin as Taoiseach Micheál Martin hosts the ninth meeting of the European Political Community (EPC).

It is part of Ireland’s six-month presidency of the EU Council.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Dublin on Wednesday night and had talks with Mr Martin, then thanked Ireland for its “unwavering support”.

Mr Zelensky said he expects to receive an update from US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner after recent talks with Russia in Abu Dhabi.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is among leaders set to arrive on Thursday, flying in after attending the UN Cop31 climate conference in Turkey.

He is expected to announce further sanctions against Russia and discuss hybrid threats to European security.

At the EPC summit, Mr Burnham is expected to co-chair a security and defence roundtable, attend an Ukraine meeting and hold a series of bilateral talks.

He has recently reopened the debate about Britain’s future relationship with the EU and ahead of a summit in Brussels next Friday.

Mr Burnham’s spokesman told reporters on Wednesday: “You can expect a focus on Ukraine, particularly following the peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week, and of course the EU summit.

“The Prime Minister will use the meeting of more than 50 leaders to drive forward both agendas to boost security in Europe and here at home and make progress through an EU deal that cuts costs for families.”

The EPC was set up in 2022 as an informal forum for leaders to hold political and strategic discussions on issues of shared concern, after the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

This will be its ninth meeting and will involve leaders from all EU countries, the wider European region, EU institutions and international organisations.

The theme of the summit in Dublin is “Europe – strong, secure and connected”, and it will include discussions on strengthening Europe’s economy in the face of geopolitical challenges, supporting Ukraine and addressing hybrid threats, efforts to undermine democracy and AI.

The gathering will be chaired by the president of the European Council, António Costa.

news.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Future in Limbo Amid Reported Second Affair
news.text: Jensen Huang’s hold on Nvidia, the company he built into the engine of the artificial intelligence boom, is in doubt Wednesday, as reports of a second extramarital affair compounded an alleged spy scandal that has drawn scrutiny from Washington to Wall Street. The reversal was swift. On Sunday, as it opened an independent inquiry into reports that Jensen Huang had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort," the board said in a statement that it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised." It added: "The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team." That confidence lasted three days. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that the board was preparing to push Jensen Huang out after two extramarital affairs, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy, and that directors could meet as soon as Wednesday. Newsweek reached out to Nvidia via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know Reports of a second relationship surfaced only hours earlier, in The New York Times, citing five people who had worked at Nvidia. The outlet reported that Jensen Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care, who reports to him. Two of those people told the Times the pair were filmed being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's developer conference in March; the paper said it had not seen the footage. According to three people briefed on the episode, the Times reported that Jensen Huang's security detail isolated the bystander who recorded it and offered that person a nondisclosure agreement. When the Times reached Jensen Huang by phone, he said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," and hung up, the paper reported. Powell did not immediately respond to the Times. Both are married to other people, the outlet highlighted. In October, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia chips, was gathering information for Beijing, and had grown close to the Nvidia chief. The two are not related. The Associated Press reported that a Commerce Department inquiry into whether Megaspeed routed advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users was handed to the Justice Department's National Security Division, which is also scrutinizing Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter. Megaspeed has denied the allegations. Beijing has dismissed them outright: "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday. Jensen Huang admitted the affair Sunday in a message to employees and did not name the woman. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," he wrote in part about his wife. The same day, a Nvidia spokesperson said Jensen Huang was "committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption." At a briefing Monday, President Donald Trump said he had called Jensen Huang “just to see if he’s feeling all right,” and that Jensen Huang said he “had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter “in terms of something else,” adding, “I think that he’ll be in good shape." “I just think he’s a very honorable man,” Trump said. Amid reports that the board is planning to oust the Nvidia founder and CEO on Wednesday, CBS News reports the Trump administration is aware of the matter. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both parties have called for investigations. Democratic U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren has asked Jensen Huang to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, which he has refused to do as of publication time. In a joint statement, Warren and Republican U.S. Senator Jim Banks said in part that Nvidia had reportedly won approval to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military,” and said the affair “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related.” A class-action lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California accuses Nvidia and Jensen Huang of artificially inflating the company’s share price by failing to disclose the affair. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Nvidia’s board weighs Jensen Huang’s future amid reports of two affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy.

news.title: ‘Trump and His Envoys Are Working for Putin, Not the US,’ Top Democrats Warn
news.text:
Three senior US Democratic lawmakers sharply condemned President Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Wednesday, Nov. 11, accusing them of undermining Ukraine’s ability to resist Russia’s invasion, pressuring Kyiv to surrender sovereign territory and promoting Kremlin demands that threaten NATO and US national security.

In a strongly worded joint statement, Congressman Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee; Congressman Adam Smith, ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee; and Senator Jack Reed, ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sharply condemned the envoys for undermining Ukraine while advancing Russian interests.

“Ukraine continues to inflict massive casualties on the Russian Army and cripple the Russian economy, while US Special Envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff continue to undermine Ukraine’s ability to negotiate a just and lasting settlement in Putin’s brutal and illegal invasion,” the lawmakers said.

They also warned that the envoys’ actions threatened NATO, which they described as “the most successful alliance in history.”

“Their parroting of Kremlin talking points on renegotiating European security and possibly pulling back from Eastern Europe is totally unacceptable to the continued viability of NATO and the national security of the United States,” the statement said.

Democrats condemn pressure to surrender Ukraine’s fortified defenses

The lawmakers accused Kushner and Witkoff of repeatedly pressuring Kyiv to surrender sovereign Ukrainian territory, including its heavily fortified defensive positions in Donbas.

“This is in addition to the constant pressure from Kushner and Witkoff for Kyiv to surrender sovereign Ukrainian territory, including its fortress belt – key defensive positions preventing a rapid advance westward,” they said.

The statement accused the envoys of repeatedly bypassing, ignoring and undermining the US intelligence community and State Department.

“Their Trumpian transactional approach, in which they are treating a nation’s fight for survival like a real estate deal, threatens global stability,” the lawmakers said.

“They and Trump are working for Putin, not for the benefit of the people of the United States.”

The accusations came as President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected US pressure to surrender territory in Donbas during a press conference in Dublin.

“The American side very often raises the topic of Donbas, part of our Ukrainian land,” Zelensky said Wednesday.

“They think that to end this war, we have to leave our territory. It’s impossible to talk this way with us, with an independent, sovereign country.”

‘Putin responds only to strength’

Meeks, Smith and Reed warned that weakening Ukraine while easing pressure on Moscow would not produce a lasting peace but would instead reward Russian aggression.

“Congress and the American people also understand that Putin responds only to strength,” they said.

“Negotiating away all the pressure from him while undercutting Ukraine has not and will never be successful.”

The lawmakers also condemned proposals that could undermine NATO’s post-Cold War security arrangements by accommodating Russian demands for a reduced Western military presence in Eastern Europe.

“Pushing a post-war security agreement that seeks to destroy NATO’s post-Cold War mandate of a ‘Europe whole, free, and at peace,’ benefits only Russia and threatens grave consequences for us and the rest of the world,” they warned.

They argued that Congress and the American public had historically supported Ukraine and NATO because doing so was both strategically sound and morally right.

The lawmakers also criticized what they described as the administration’s focus on transactional diplomacy at the expense of America’s national security interests.

Democrats warn Trump against ‘appeasing Putin’

The statement came ahead of Thursday’s planned meeting between Kushner, Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

As Kyiv Post reported, the envoys are expected to meet Putin before traveling to Dublin for further negotiations with Zelensky.

The Ukrainian president has expressed skepticism that Moscow will provide concrete answers to proposals discussed during Abu Dhabi talks, while insisting that Washington must pressure Russia rather than demand territorial concessions from Ukraine.

Zelensky also stressed that Kyiv needs binding security guarantees from the US, not promises from Moscow.

The Democratic lawmakers concluded their statement with a direct warning to Trump, accusing his envoys of pursuing an approach that risks rewarding Russia’s invasion.

“The Administration has claimed to be in favor of ‘peace through strength.’ The president should inform Kushner and Witkoff that surrendering in Ukraine and appeasing Putin will result in neither peace nor strength.”
news.summary: Top congressional Democrats sharply condemn Trump, Kushner and Witkoff for undermining Ukraine, pressuring Kyiv to surrender sovereign territory and promoting Kremlin demands that threaten NATO and US national security.

news.title: Senators fire opening shot at Trump aides over Nvidia CEO’s suspected spy affair: WSJ
news.text:
Two incoming Senate committee chairs took aim at President Donald Trump's top aides over a scandal swirling around one of his tech allies.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) are demanding that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve every record tied to Nvidia's chip sales to China and CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.

The senators gave the three officials until Tuesday to confirm they've told their staffs to hold onto all communications and other materials. Warren and Coons pointed to their incoming posts atop the Senate Banking and Foreign Relations committees, which oversee sensitive tech exports and national security.

The Journal noted that such letters tend to come before a formal congressional investigation. This letter arrives alongside a flood of similar demands aimed at companies and organizations closely tied to the administration.

The situation "raises significant concerns about the federal government's ability to effectively enforce our export controls," the pair wrote, adding that it also puts national security at risk.

They're seeking security and intelligence files on the suspected Chinese operation and Huang, any communications between Nvidia and the administration, including Huang's dealings with Trump himself, and records on chip export policy.

Huang forged a close bond with the president and personally pressed him to let Nvidia ship chips straight to China, all while carrying on an affair with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based data-center firm Megaspeed International, The Journal reported. Nvidia's board was preparing to push him out over that affair and a second extramarital relationship, according to The Journal.

Warren and Coons have spent the past two years hammering Huang and the administration's decision to green-light chip shipments to China and other high-risk nations such as the United Arab Emirates.

The backlash isn't limited to Democrats. National Economic Council Director Larry Kudlow and Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-ND) had both urged Huang to resign by early Wednesday, while House Republicans, including Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast (R-FL), want Huang to brief lawmakers next week and have said they're open to subpoenaing him.

Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-WA) went further, noting that Huang's signature motorcycle jacket has earned him a nickname in China and saying he hoped Congress wouldn't have to trade it for prison stripes over potential espionage or export control violations.
